# Buckleson

Buckleson is a blockchain infrastructure company. We build custom blockchains, tokenize real-world assets, launch crypto wallets and protect AI agents.

---

## About Buckleson

URL: https://buckleson.com/about/

Buckleson is a blockchain infrastructure company, not a crypto company. We rebuild systems where traditional technology cannot solve the problem, such as shared records, private data and payments that must be safe and cheap. Today, we use blockchain to protect the new, AI-driven internet.

Founder: Vijay Tadepalli, Founder.

### Our story

- It started with a wallet. Our first product was a crypto wallet and exchange in one app. Today it is Hyper Wallet.

- We found the hidden charges. Many wallets earn money from charges that users do not see. Examples are a worse price on each swap or a wallet fee on top of the exchange fee. We wanted to remove these charges, not hide them better.

- So we built our own blockchain. Hyper 0X runs an order book inside its consensus. The chain matches buy and sell orders itself, like an exchange that no single party runs. Users pay one fee, not two.

- We fixed the blockchain trilemma. Most blockchains give up decentralization, scalability or security. We took an idea from microservices. Each application or policy gets its own L2, and one shared L1 does the final settlement and audit. L3s on top of an L2 are coming soon.

- Then we saw it was never only about payments. A record that nobody can secretly change is useful far beyond money. We took Hyper 0X to tokenized assets, to processes that many companies share, and to identity checks that keep personal data private.

- Today, we build security for AI agents. AI agents now read files, call tools and move money, and people give them private data every day. Pavii puts every agent call through six gates and keeps a receipt on Hyper 0X that nobody can secretly change. All our work comes together here.

We believe blockchain is one of the most underrated technologies. Payments are only the start.

### Our vision

We want to make the internet safe again. AI is everywhere, and people give it their private data every day. We believe privacy can be real again, not a myth.

AI is now part of almost every app. People share personal data with it, and attacks follow that data. A normal database asks you to trust whoever owns it.

A blockchain lets a company prove a fact and keep a record that nobody can secretly change, without showing the data behind it. I started Buckleson to build that layer of trust for the AI era.

### Mission, vision, goal and moat

- Mission: Solve what a database cannot. We use blockchain where a normal database is not enough: records that many companies share, privacy with proof, and ownership that everyone can check.

- Vision: Records that nobody can secretly change. We want critical systems to run on shared records that nobody can secretly edit, while each person keeps control of their own data.

- Goal: A blockchain for every application. We want any company to start its own chain as easily as a cloud server. Each application gets a private L2, with settlement and audit on one shared L1.

- Moat: We own every layer. We built the L1, the L2s, the wallet and the AI security gateway ourselves. So we control fees, roadmap and security, and we test every idea in our own products first.

### Where blockchain does what a database cannot

A database works when one company owns the data and everyone trusts that company. Many real problems have no such owner. That is where a blockchain helps.

- Prove a fact, keep the data private: Check that a customer passed identity checks, is old enough or has enough funds, without seeing their documents. The proof is enough, and the data stays with its owner.

- Run one process across many companies: A shipment, a loan or an insurance claim can involve five companies. On a shared ledger, each party sees the same steps and only its own private data. Nobody has to own the database.

- Own a part of a large asset: Split a building, a fund or a bar of gold into small units. Each owner can prove what they own, and units trade and settle in one step.

- Audit without exposing everything: Each party keeps its records encrypted, and the ledger keeps a fingerprint of each one. An auditor can confirm that nothing changed and read only what it has a key for.

- Rules that run before money moves: Limits, approvals and identity checks run before a transaction executes. A breach does not happen, so nobody has to undo it later.

- AI agents that you can audit: Every action of an AI agent leaves a signed receipt on the chain. Nobody can secretly change it, so you can give agents real work.

Q: Who founded Buckleson?
A: Vijay Tadepalli founded Buckleson. The company started with a crypto wallet, Hyper Wallet, and then built its own blockchain, Hyper 0X.

Q: Why did Buckleson build its own blockchain?
A: Many wallets earn money from hidden charges. Buckleson built Hyper 0X with an order book inside its consensus, so users pay one fee, not two. Then the team made it modular: a private L2 for each application and one shared L1 for settlement and audit.

Q: What can a blockchain do besides payments?
A: A blockchain can prove a fact without showing private data. It lets many companies run one process on a shared record. It splits large assets into small units that owners can verify. It also runs rules before a transaction executes and keeps a record of AI agent actions that nobody can secretly change.

Q: How does Hyper 0X handle the blockchain trilemma?
A: Hyper 0X splits the work, like microservices. Each application gets its own L2, so it can grow alone, and L3s on top of an L2 are coming soon. The shared L1 does the final settlement and audit with leaderless consensus, so no single node sets the order of transactions.

---

## Hyper 0X (coming soon)

URL: https://buckleson.com/products/hyper-0x/

Hyper 0X is the blockchain that Buckleson built from the start. Each customer gets a private L2 with its own rules. Every L2 settles on one shared L1. Each transaction is final in one pass. Every connection is post-quantum-resistant, and compliance rules run before a transaction executes.

- Final in one pass: Consensus has no leader and gives deterministic finality. It never reorders or undoes a transaction, and it has no single leader to attack.

- Post-quantum-resistant: Every connection uses a hybrid key exchange (ML-KEM-768 with X25519). Data stays encrypted in transit, in use, on the ledger and at rest.

- A private L2 for every customer: You get your own sequencer, rules, privacy and bridge. Blocks grow when traffic is high and shrink when it is low, so no queue builds up.

- Compliance as code: The chain checks limits, KYC and maker-checker approvals before a transaction executes, not after.

- No seed phrases: With account abstraction, users sign in with a face scan or a passkey. Apps can pay the network fees for their users.

- Connects to other chains: Bridge adapters connect to EVM chains, Solana and Sui. SDKs connect to bank ledgers and core banking APIs.

- Consensus: Asynchronous BFT based on hashgraph, with known validators bound to PKI certificates. The network stays safe while fewer than one third of validators are faulty.

- Transaction ordering: Each transaction gets the median time at which the validators received it. No single node decides the order.

- Encryption: TLS 1.3 with hybrid X25519 and ML-KEM-768, AES-256-GCM, a separate encrypted payload for each party, and master keys in an HSM.

- Smart contracts: Write contracts in Rust. A TypeScript framework is in development. Deploy to the L1 or to any L2. Upgrades need approval.

- AI audit trail: The chain can record AI decisions and actions as signed, chained transactions for audits, billing and disputes.

- Network type: A permissioned L1. Each customer has an L2 that posts its state roots to the L1.

- L3s (coming soon): An L3 will run on top of an L2, for one application or one policy. It will settle on its L2, and the L2 settles on the L1.

Q: What is Hyper 0X?
A: Hyper 0X is an enterprise blockchain that Buckleson built. It is a permissioned L1 with deterministic finality and post-quantum-resistant encryption. Every customer runs on its own private L2.

Q: Is Hyper 0X a public or private blockchain?
A: The L1 is permissioned: all validators are known and bound to PKI certificates. Each customer L2 is private, with its own rules, and settles on the shared L1. Bridges connect it to public chains such as Ethereum, Solana and Sui.

Q: Can I launch my own chain on Hyper 0X?
A: Yes, when Hyper 0X launches. Hyper 0X is under development. Buckleson will set up an L2 for you with your own sequencer, compliance rules, privacy settings and bridges. Then we will help you move from a pilot to production.

## Pavii (coming soon)

URL: https://buckleson.com/products/pavii/

Pavii sits between your AI agents and your systems. Every call from Claude, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok or your own agents passes six security gates. The rules and the receipts are on Hyper 0X, so nobody can secretly change or delete a record of what an agent did. Pavii also cuts token use by 30 to 60 percent.

- Connect any agent: Connect Claude, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode and your own agents through one gateway.

- Blocks prompt injection: Pavii treats untrusted text as data, not as instructions. A detector finds injected instructions, and a contract on the chain stops them.

- Stops data leaks: A privacy gate removes personal data and secrets before a model can see them.

- Tamper-proof receipts: Pavii chains each log entry to the one before it and anchors the chain on Hyper 0X. If someone deletes an entry, you see exactly what is missing.

- Fewer tokens: On a measured Claude Code task, agents used 30 to 60 percent fewer tokens.

- Kill switch for rogue agents: An agent that breaks rules moves from observed, to restricted, to stopped. A person can stop any agent at any time.

- Prompt injection: Pavii finds and blocks injected instructions in web pages, files and tool output.

- Sensitive data leaks: Pavii removes personal data and secrets from what goes in and from what comes out.

- Supply chain: Every new package or MCP server must pass an allow-list, a pinned hash or a sandbox test.

- Unsafe output: Pavii removes scripts and secrets from agent output before delivery.

- Excessive agency: An egress smart contract on Hyper 0X decides what an agent can send and do.

- Runaway cost: Budgets and MCP compaction keep token use under control.

Q: What does Pavii do?
A: Pavii is a security gateway for AI agents. It checks every agent call against six gates: injection, privacy, supply chain, budget, egress and output. It records the rules and the receipts on the Hyper 0X blockchain.

Q: Which AI agents does Pavii support?
A: Pavii supports Claude, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode and custom agents. You can connect the subscriptions that you already have.

Q: Why use a blockchain for AI security?
A: Nobody can secretly edit or delete logs and rules on a blockchain. Every agent action leaves a signed receipt. Auditors, billing teams and dispute teams can check that receipt.

## Hyper Wallet & SDKs (coming soon)

URL: https://buckleson.com/products/hyper-wallet/

Hyper Wallet is one non-custodial app to hold, swap and trade crypto and tokenized assets on many chains. Users pay one fee, not two. The same wallet will also come as SDKs. Banks and fintechs will use them to launch their own wallet, neobank or payment gateway on Hyper 0X.

- Multi-chain, non-custodial: Use Bitcoin, Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, Tron, TON, XRP, Stellar, Sui and more. Your keys stay on your device.

- Swap and trade in one place: Swap from any coin page on the best route. Each swap has MEV protection, and both sides settle at the same time.

- Perps, pre-IPO and index funds: Trade perpetual futures. Invest in tokenized pre-IPO stocks and index funds from the same app.

- Markets beyond coins: See coins, pump.fun tokens, tokenized assets such as gold and stocks, and Polymarket prediction markets.

- Deposit from exchanges: Add funds from Binance or Coinbase on any coin page. The app fills in your address for you.

- White-label SDKs: Put wallets, payments and a payment gateway with your brand into your own app or game.

- On-chain order book: A central limit order book runs inside Hyper 0X consensus. Every validator calculates the same fills, so nobody can trade ahead of an order.

- Atomic settlement: Both sides of a trade settle in one step, or neither side settles. No side is left exposed.

- One fee, not two: Users pay one transaction cost. They do not pay an exchange fee and then a wallet fee.

- dApps and NFTs: Connect to dApps through WalletConnect. Keep your NFTs next to your coins.

- Simple status: Users see only three states: pending, confirmed or failed. They do not compare records across apps.

Q: Is Hyper Wallet custodial?
A: No. Hyper Wallet is non-custodial: the private keys stay on the device of the user. A business that needs custody can add it through the SDKs.

Q: Which blockchains does Hyper Wallet support?
A: Hyper Wallet supports Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dash, Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, Tron, TON, XRP, Stellar and Sui. Hyper 0X bridges connect it to more chains.

Q: Can I launch my own branded wallet?
A: Yes, when the SDKs launch. Hyper Wallet is under development. With the SDKs, banks, fintechs and apps will put the wallet, payments and a payment gateway into their own app, with their own brand.

## HyperRun (coming soon)

URL: https://buckleson.com/products/hyperrun/

HyperRun is coming soon. It is a realistic first-person shooter. Players earn money when they play and win. Fans earn when they predict matches correctly. Fans can also sponsor good players. The game signs every result, and payouts settle on Hyper 0X.

- Earn by playing: Players earn money when they play and when they win.

- In-game predictions: Predict the results of matches and players. Earn when your prediction is correct.

- Player sponsorship: Other players back good players through their predictions, and the good players get sponsorship.

- Signed match results: The game signs every result before any payout. Nobody can change a result after the game signs it.

- Rewards contract: A smart contract on Hyper 0X settles the predictions and pays the winners.

- In-game wallet: Players and fans get a wallet that uses the Hyper Wallet SDK.

## Frequently asked questions

URL: https://buckleson.com/faq/

Q: What does Buckleson do?
A: Buckleson is a blockchain infrastructure company. We built our own blockchain, Hyper 0X. On it, we deliver custom blockchains, asset tokenization, crypto wallets and exchanges, and security for AI agents.

Q: Can you build a custom blockchain for my company?
A: Yes, that is our core service. We set up a private L2 on Hyper 0X with your own rules, privacy and bridges. We connect it to your systems and support you from the pilot to production.

Q: How does Hyper 0X keep each customer's data private?
A: Every customer runs on its own L2, so its transactions never mix with the transactions of others. Data stays encrypted in transit, in use, on the ledger and at rest. Only the parties to a record hold the keys to read it.

Q: Will Pavii block the tool calls my agents need?
A: No. Pavii stops only a call that breaks a rule. Examples are an injected instruction, personal data that leaves, an unknown package, an empty budget or a destination that is not allowed. Allowed calls go through, and every decision gets a receipt.

Q: Why is a blockchain more secure for my business?
A: Nobody can secretly edit or delete records on Hyper 0X. Every connection is post-quantum-resistant. Compliance rules run before a transaction executes. So auditors and regulators get one record that they can check.

Q: Who do you work with?
A: We work with banks and fintechs, asset issuers and AI or enterprise security teams. Most start with one use case, such as a payment flow, a tokenized asset or a group of AI agents. Then they grow from there.

Q: How do we start working with you?
A: Book a 30-minute call. We learn what you want to put on a blockchain. Then we propose a pilot on your own L2, with a clear scope and clear success measures.

Q: When do your products launch?
A: Hyper 0X, Pavii, Hyper Wallet, H0X Pay and HyperRun are under development and coming soon. Book a call to learn more.

### Blockchain for business

Q: Is a private blockchain just a shared database?
A: No, not when several organisations must share one record and no single one must control it. A database has one owner who can change any row. A permissioned blockchain gives every participant a copy, and known validators agree on each change. History is tamper-evident. If only one company writes the data and everyone trusts it, use a normal database.

Q: When should a company not use a blockchain?
A: Do not use a blockchain when one party owns the data, nobody else checks it and records change often. A blockchain is useful when several parties must trust the same record. It is also useful when settlement must be final, or when an auditor needs proof that nobody changed a record later.

Q: How does consensus work on an enterprise blockchain?
A: The validators are organisations that everyone knows, and each one has an identity certificate. They use a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol to agree on the next block. The protocol continues to work when some validators fail or act badly. Hyper 0X uses asynchronous BFT with deterministic finality: when the validators agree on a block, it is final in one pass.

Q: Should a company launch its own L1 or an L2?
A: Most companies need an L2. To run an L1, you must find and coordinate independent validators for years. An L2 gives you your own rules, privacy and capacity, and a shared L1 gives security and settlement. On Hyper 0X, every customer gets a private L2, and we run the L1 for them.

Q: How does a blockchain handle GDPR and the right to be forgotten?
A: Do not put readable personal data on the ledger. Keep the data off the chain or encrypted. Put only a reference or a fingerprint on the chain. When a person asks for deletion, destroy the key, and the data becomes unreadable. Regulators still change their guidance, so get legal advice for your case.

Q: What decides how much a private blockchain costs?
A: The scope decides the cost more than the technology. Count the organisations that take part, the systems to connect, the compliance rules to apply and the security reviews to do. A chain on an existing L1 costs much less infrastructure than a new chain. A small pilot is the cheapest way to get a real number.

### AI-agent security

Q: What actually works against prompt injection?
A: Use layers, because no single filter catches every attack. Check inputs and tool outputs for injected instructions. Give each agent only the permissions that its task needs. Limit where it can send data, and get a person to approve risky actions. Log everything. Then an injected agent cannot do real damage.

Q: How do you enforce permissions on AI agent tool calls?
A: Put a gateway between the agents and the tools. The gateway checks each call against the policy for that agent. The policy sets the tools, the valid arguments, the data that can leave and the spend limit. Calls that pass go through. The gateway blocks the other calls, gives a reason and logs the decision.

Q: How do you stop AI agents from running up huge bills?
A: Give every agent its own budget, and enforce it outside the model. Set token and spend limits for each task and each day. Limit retries, find loops and compact the context. A provider dashboard shows the spend after it happens. A gateway stops the call before it happens.

Q: How do you monitor AI agents that take real actions?
A: Record every action: who asked, which agent acted, what it had permission to do and what happened. Chain each entry to the entry before it, and anchor the chain on a blockchain. Then a deleted or changed entry shows as a gap.

Q: What is excessive agency in AI?
A: Excessive agency is one of the top security risks for apps built on large language models. It means that an agent has more functions, permissions or freedom than its task needs. Then a mistake or an injected instruction can cause real damage. To prevent it, give the least permissions, use narrow tools and get approval for actions with a high impact.

Q: How do companies stop sensitive data reaching external AI models?
A: Send all model traffic through one gateway. The gateway finds personal data and secrets and removes them before a prompt leaves. It also records who sent which data to which model. Then block AI tools that are not approved at the edge of the network.

Q: Can an AI agent be trusted to spend money?
A: Yes, but only inside limits that the agent cannot change. Give it a fixed budget and a list of allowed payees. Get a person to approve payments above a set amount, and keep a receipt for every payment. Keep these rules outside the agent, for example as a contract on a ledger. Then a compromised agent still cannot spend too much.

### Asset tokenization

Q: What is the difference between asset tokenization and security tokenization?
A: Asset tokenization is the general idea: you show any asset, such as gold, invoices or property, as a digital token. A security token is a tokenized asset that is a security by law. So securities rules apply when you issue, sell and transfer it.

Q: Which blockchain is best for tokenizing assets?
A: Check five things. Check privacy for holders and final settlement. Check that compliance controls are part of each transfer. Check that the chain connects to the places where the asset will trade. Check that you can hold the operator to account. Regulated issuers often use a permissioned chain with bridges to public networks.

Q: Is owning a token the same as owning the asset?
A: Only if the legal documents say so. A token is a record. Its rights come from the legal structure behind it, often a special purpose vehicle that holds the asset. Good tokenization connects the record on the chain to legal rights that a court can enforce.

Q: What is the hardest part of tokenizing real-world assets?
A: The technology is rarely the hardest part. The hard parts are the legal structure, the custody of the asset, the onboarding of investors and real demand for the token. Plan these first. Write the smart contracts last.

### Wallets for business

Q: How can I tell if a wallet is really non-custodial?
A: Ask who can move the funds without the user. If the provider holds a key, or a key share that it can combine with another share it controls, the wallet is really custodial. In a non-custodial wallet, only the keys or devices of the user can approve a transfer.

Q: What is the difference between MPC, multisig and smart account wallets?
A: An MPC wallet splits one private key into shares that different parties hold. A multisig wallet needs several separate keys to approve a transaction, and the chain enforces this rule. A smart account is a contract wallet with rules that you can program, such as spending limits, recovery and paid gas. Many business wallets use more than one of these.

Q: What is the difference between ERC-4337 and EIP-7702?
A: ERC-4337 adds smart contract accounts to Ethereum without a change to the protocol. It uses a separate flow of user operations. EIP-7702 has been live since the Pectra upgrade in 2025. It lets a normal account delegate to smart contract code, so existing addresses can get smart-account features.

Q: Can you recover crypto if you lose your seed phrase?
A: Usually not. Paid recovery services that promise to recover your crypto are a common scam. The solution is prevention. A smart account can add recovery through trusted devices, guardians or a passkey. Then a lost phone does not mean lost funds.

Q: Are passkeys safe for crypto wallets?
A: Yes, when the wallet supports them correctly. A passkey signs with a key that never leaves secure hardware, and nobody can steal it with a fake login page. A synced passkey is easier to recover. A passkey on one device is stricter. A good wallet adds a separate recovery path to both types.

### Post-quantum security

Q: Can quantum computers break blockchains?
A: They can break some parts. A large quantum computer can forge the digital signatures that protect wallets today. Hash functions are much stronger against it. Also, an attacker can record encrypted data today and decrypt it later. This risk is largest for private enterprise records.

Q: Is Bitcoin quantum resistant?
A: Not yet. Bitcoin signatures use elliptic-curve cryptography, and a large quantum computer can break it. The risk is highest for coins whose public keys are already visible on the chain. A move to post-quantum signatures needs an upgrade of the full network, and that is still under discussion.

Q: Is SHA-256 safe against quantum computers?
A: Mostly, yes. The best known quantum attack on hash functions, Grover's algorithm, cuts the effective security in half. SHA-256 still keeps a very large margin. Signatures and key exchange are the parts to replace.

Q: What is ML-KEM?
A: ML-KEM is the post-quantum standard for key encapsulation. NIST published it as FIPS 203 in August 2024, and it is based on the Kyber algorithm. Two parties use it to agree on a shared secret. Nobody knows a way for a quantum computer to break it.

Q: Why combine X25519 with ML-KEM instead of using ML-KEM alone?
A: Two locks are safer than one. X25519 has resisted classical attacks for decades. ML-KEM is designed to resist quantum attacks. A hybrid key exchange stays secure while either one holds. So if someone finds a flaw in the newer algorithm later, your data stays protected. Hyper 0X uses this hybrid on every connection.

Q: Do we need post-quantum encryption now?
A: Yes, if your data must stay secret for years. Attackers can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it when quantum computers are ready. Add the years that your data must stay secret to the years that a migration takes. If that total is longer than the time until such computers exist, you are already late.

---

## What Can Blockchain Do Beyond Payments and Crypto?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/blockchain-use-cases-beyond-payments/

Beyond payments, a blockchain gives several organizations one shared record that no single company owns and nobody can quietly rewrite. On that record, companies can prove facts without sharing private data, run one process together and split the ownership of real assets. They can also check records without reading them, run rules before a transaction executes, trace goods and hold AI agents to account. Crypto is one use of blockchain, not the whole of it.

## What are the main blockchain use cases beyond payments?

| Use case | Example | Why one database falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Prove a fact, keep the data | "This customer passed identity checks" | Documents get copied to each checker |
| Shared process | One shipment, six companies | One company owns the record |
| Fractional ownership | A made-up $2M warehouse, 2,000 tokens | Every broker keeps its own register |
| Check without reading | An audit of encrypted records | The auditor must trust the admin |
| Rules before execution | Fund tokens for verified investors only | The owner can switch rules off unseen |
| Provenance | One invoice, one loan | Each bank sees only its own loans |
| Accountable AI agents | A receipt for every agent action | Admins and agents can edit logs |
| Payments | Cash and asset in one step | The two legs settle apart |

## How can a blockchain prove a fact without revealing the data?

A blockchain can hold proof of a fact while the data stays private. Today, a firm that checks a new customer often asks for copies of the passport. Each copy can leak.

A zero-knowledge proof removes the copies. It is a piece of math that proves a statement is true and reveals nothing else. A bank checks the passport once and signs a statement. The customer then proves "a bank verified me" without the passport, or "I am over 18" without a birth date. The proof needs no blockchain.

The blockchain gives every checker one shared place to see who signed the statement and whether the signer withdrew it. With one database, every checker must ask its owner, who then sees every check. Our guide on [how to verify a customer without seeing their data](../verify-customers-without-sharing-data/) shows the full design.

## How do several companies run one process on a blockchain?

On a blockchain, each company signs its own steps on one shared record, and the same rules run for all. Shipments, syndicated loans from many lenders and insurance claims all cross company lines. Today, each party keeps its own copy, and staff match the copies by hand.

A rule can pay the exporter when the port signs that the goods arrived. A central database can hold these steps too, but its owner can change the rules or the history. Competitors rarely accept that.

## What is fractional ownership on a blockchain?

Fractional ownership splits one asset into small pieces that people can trade. A token, a digital unit on a blockchain, stands for each piece. Take a made-up $2M warehouse split into 2,000 tokens of $1,000 each. A legal vehicle holds the building.

Today, each broker and custodian keeps its own register, so trades take days to settle. On a shared ledger, everyone reads one register, and the token and the cash move in one step. A token does not create buyers or fix a weak legal structure. See our [asset tokenization guide](../asset-tokenization-guide/) and our post on [tokenized bonds](../tokenized-bonds-explained/).

## How can auditors check records without reading them?

A ledger can hold a fingerprint of each record instead of the record itself. A fingerprint, or hash, is a short code that a formula computes from the data. Change one character, and the fingerprint changes. Nobody can rebuild the record from it.

At audit time, a bank reveals one record, and the auditor checks it against its original fingerprint. The other records stay encrypted. A token can also show its total supply, one half of [proof of reserve](../proof-of-reserve-explained/), while each holder record stays private. In one database, an admin can change a row and its log together, so the auditor must trust the admin.

## Can a blockchain enforce compliance rules before a transaction?

Yes. With [compliance as code](../compliance-as-code-blockchain/), the chain checks rules before a transaction executes. Typical rules are KYC (know your customer) identity checks, limits and maker-checker approvals, where a second person approves. A transfer that breaks a rule never reaches the ledger. For example, only verified investors can hold a fund token.

A database can check rules before a write too, but its owner can switch a rule off unseen. On a shared chain, every member can read the rules, and no single member can change them alone.

## How does blockchain prove where goods and documents come from?

A blockchain records each handover of a gold bar, a drug batch or a shipping document as a signed entry. Buyers can then trace its provenance: where it came from and who held it. Separate databases break that trail at each company. A blockchain cannot see a physical object, though. If a supplier records false data, the ledger keeps a false claim, signed by that supplier.

The same idea protects documents. Picture a supplier that shows one made-up $500,000 invoice to two banks and gets two loans, so one loan has nothing behind it. Neither bank can see the loan of the other. With a shared ledger of invoice fingerprints, the second bank finds a match before it pays. It sees the match, not the loan terms or the clients of the first bank.

## How does blockchain make AI agents accountable?

A blockchain records each action of an AI agent as a signed receipt that links to the one before it. A deleted entry leaves a visible gap. Agents now send emails, move data and run code. After a mistake, the company must prove what the agent did. Normal logs sit on the systems that the agent touches, so an admin or a hijacked agent can edit them. [Proof of execution for AI](../proof-of-execution-ai/) shows how receipts serve audits, billing and disputes.

## Is blockchain still useful for payments?

Yes. A blockchain can settle a payment and an asset transfer [in one step](../atomic-settlement/), so nobody pays without getting the asset. Banks can also issue [tokenized deposits](../tokenized-deposits-vs-stablecoins/). Payments are a strong use, but only one of many.

## When is a blockchain the wrong tool?

A blockchain adds cost and complexity. A normal database is the better tool when:

- One company owns the data, and everyone trusts that company.
- The data changes often, or you must delete it on request.
- Speed and cheap storage matter more than a shared history.
- Nobody outside your company will ever check the record.

Our [blockchain vs database](../blockchain-vs-database/) guide has the full decision.

## How does Hyper 0X support these use cases?

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/) is the Buckleson blockchain: one [permissioned](../permissioned-vs-permissionless-blockchain/) L1 with known validators, each bound to a certificate. Each customer gets a private L2, a private blockchain that settles on the shared L1, with its own rules, privacy and bridge. Consensus has no leader, so no single node sets the order. Each transaction is final in one pass, with no reorgs (rewrites of recent blocks).

[Per-party encryption](../blockchain-data-encryption-four-layers/) keeps each record readable only by its parties. Hash commitments on the ledger let an auditor confirm that a record did not change. Compliance as code checks limits, KYC and maker-checker approvals before a transaction executes. The invoice check above can be one of these rules, so a second loan fails before it executes.

[Pavii](../../products/pavii/), our security gateway for AI agents, checks every agent call at six gates and anchors its hash-chained receipts on Hyper 0X. Our [custom blockchain](../../services/custom-blockchains/) and [asset tokenization](../../services/asset-tokenization/) services build these systems with you.

Buckleson started with a crypto wallet, [Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/), and then built Hyper 0X. Its design comes from microservices, small services that each do one job. Each application or policy gets its own L2, with final settlement and audit on the L1. In our view, blockchain is the most underrated technology in business.

For AI security in detail, read [how to secure AI agents](../how-to-secure-ai-agents/).

## Where should you start?

1. List the records that you and your partners copy back and forth.
2. Mark what partners must check and what they must never see.
3. Pick one process with clear pain, such as slow matching, disputes or double financing.
4. Write the rules that every transaction in that process must pass.
5. Run a pilot on one private L2, and measure the work that it removes.

## Blockchain vs Database: When Do You Need a Blockchain?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/blockchain-vs-database/

You need a blockchain when several organizations write to one shared record and none of them trusts a single owner to control it. The blockchain then gives them a history that nobody can rewrite alone. If one company owns the data and everyone trusts that company, a normal database is faster, cheaper and simpler. Many systems use both: a database for private, fast-changing data, and a blockchain for the facts that several parties share.

## What is the difference between a blockchain and a database?

The main difference is control. One owner runs a database, and an admin can change or delete any row. That makes a database fast, cheap and easy to fix.

A blockchain is a shared ledger that several parties run together. Validators, the computers that check and record transactions, must agree before a new entry joins it. Nobody edits old entries, so the record holds even when the parties do not trust each other.

| Question | Database | Blockchain |
|---|---|---|
| Who controls it? | One owner | Several parties, by agreement |
| Who writes to it? | The owner and its users | Each member, with its own key |
| Whom must you trust? | The owner | No single party |
| Can history change? | Yes, an admin can edit rows | No, a correction is a new entry |
| Who can read it? | The owner and its users | Everyone on public chains, only the parties on encrypted permissioned chains |
| How fast and cheap is a write? | Fast and cheap | Slower and costlier, because validators must agree |
| What is it best for? | Data that one company owns | Facts that several companies share |

## Who owns and controls the data?

If one company owns the data and answers for it alone, use a database. Payroll and a product catalog belong there.

The picture changes when a record belongs to a group. Think of a loan that five banks fund together. Someone must run the shared database, and that party gains power over the others. It can change a rule, delay an entry or read the data of a competitor. A blockchain removes that role, because no single party runs the record.

## How many parties write to the record, and do they trust each other?

One writer never needs a blockchain. Several writers who all trust one operator can share a database that the operator runs. That is often the simplest answer.

A blockchain fits when the writers do not trust each other or any operator enough. Each party signs its own entries with its own key. Consensus, the process by which validators agree on the record, decides what goes in and in what order. The writers then depend on a group of validators, not on one operator. Our post on [permissioned vs permissionless blockchains](../permissioned-vs-permissionless-blockchain/) explains who runs the validators.

## How much does rewrite risk matter for an audit?

Rewrite risk matters most when outsiders must trust your history. In a database, an admin with enough rights can edit a row and the log that records the edit. Audit tables and backups help, but the same owner controls them. So an auditor must trust the owner, or match the history against other copies.

On a blockchain, an attacker must control many validators at different organizations to rewrite history. On a chain with [final settlement](../blockchain-finality-explained/), nobody can reverse a confirmed entry at all. The auditor checks one record instead of many copies. If nobody outside your company audits the record, this benefit is worth little.

## How do privacy needs change the choice?

A database is private by default. Many public blockchains are the opposite: every node sees every transaction, so they are a poor home for client records.

A permissioned blockchain, where only approved organizations run validators, can encrypt each record for its parties. The ledger can also hold a hash, a short fingerprint of the data. Personal data needs extra care, because people can ask you to delete it. Keep it in a database, and put only its fingerprint on the chain. Check with your lawyers that this meets your obligations. See [private L2 vs public blockchain](../private-l2-vs-public-blockchain/) for the options.

## What does a blockchain cost compared with a database?

A blockchain costs more for each write. Several validators must agree on every entry, and each of them stores a copy. You also need people who can manage keys, validators and smart contracts, the programs that run on a blockchain.

The savings come from elsewhere. A shared record removes the work to match copies between companies, the disputes about whose copy is right and the fees of a middleman. So compare the cost of the chain with the cost of that work, not with a database.

## When is a database the better choice?

For most software, a database is the honest answer:

- **One owner.** One company writes the data and answers for it.
- **A trusted operator.** All parties accept one operator, and a contract holds it to account.
- **Frequent edits.** Drafts, profiles and personal data change often or must disappear.
- **Heavy queries.** Reports and search need indexes. Teams copy blockchain data into a database for this anyway.
- **High volume, low stakes.** Clicks, sensor readings and app logs rarely need a shared history.
- **No outside audit.** Nobody outside your company will ever check the record.

## How do you decide if you need a blockchain?

Answer these six questions with yes or no.

1. Do several organizations write to the same record?
2. Do they lack a neutral operator that all of them trust?
3. Does it hurt if one party rewrites the history?
4. Do auditors, regulators or partners need to check that history?
5. Can personal data stay off the ledger, with only fingerprints on it?
6. Can the parties agree on the rules that every transaction must pass?

Yes to questions 1, 2 and 3 means that a blockchain is worth a pilot. A no to any of them points to a database. Questions 4 to 6 shape the design.

## What does this look like at a lending fintech?

Picture a lending fintech that sells shares of a made-up $10M loan pool to four partner banks. Customer profiles and documents change every day, and only the fintech uses them. That data stays in its database. The loan register is different: five firms write to it, and each one must prove its share.

So the register moves to a private L2, a private blockchain that settles on the Hyper 0X main chain. Each bank signs its own entries, and each repayment is final when it joins the record. Nobody can edit a past entry. A maker-checker rule requires a second approver for each correction, so a correction without one fails before it executes. The original entry stays, and all five firms read the same history.

## How does Hyper 0X work next to a database?

On [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain, the shared record goes on a private L2, and private data stays in your database. Hyper 0X is a permissioned [L1](../layer-1-vs-layer-2-blockchain/), the main chain, with known validators, each bound to a certificate. Each L2 has its own sequencer, the node that orders its transactions, plus its own rules and bridge.

Consensus has no leader, so no single node sets the order. Each transaction is final in one pass, with no reorgs (rewrites of recent blocks). Per-party encryption keeps each record readable only by its parties. Hash commitments on the ledger let an auditor confirm that a record did not change. Compliance as code checks limits, KYC (know your customer) status and maker-checker approvals before a transaction executes. Every connection is post-quantum-resistant.

Software kits (SDKs) connect each L2 to bank ledgers and core banking APIs. Our [custom blockchain service](../../services/custom-blockchains/) builds the L2 and runs it with you. To compare partners, read [how to choose a blockchain development company](../how-to-choose-a-blockchain-development-company/). For more use cases, see [what blockchain can do beyond payments](../blockchain-use-cases-beyond-payments/).

## Where should you start?

1. Draw the record that you want to share, and list every party that writes to it.
2. Answer the first three questions of the checklist.
3. Split the data: private and personal data stay in your database, and shared facts go on the chain.
4. Write the rules that every shared transaction must pass.
5. Run a pilot on one private L2 next to your existing database.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to test your use case against this checklist.

## What Is Compliance as Code on a Blockchain?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/compliance-as-code-blockchain/

Compliance as code means that you write compliance rules, such as KYC checks, transfer limits and approvals, as code that a blockchain runs. The chain checks each transaction against the rules before the transaction executes. A transaction that fails a rule never reaches the ledger. So the firm stops a breach before it happens, instead of finding it later and unwinding it.

## Why do firms need compliance as code?

Most compliance today happens after the fact. A payment or a trade goes through first. Then a monitoring system reviews it, flags a problem and sends it to a person. Staff investigate, report the case and try to reverse the transaction. Each step costs time and money, and the breach has already happened.

On a blockchain, an after-the-fact check is a bigger problem. A blockchain is a shared ledger that many computers keep in sync. After a transaction is final, nobody can reverse it. To undo it, the firm needs a second transaction, and often the help of the other party. Compliance as code moves the check to the only safe place: before execution.

For executives, the benefit is simple. The written policy and the system behavior become the same thing. Regulators, auditors and boards can read the rules and see that the chain applies them to every transaction.

## What rules can you write as code?

You can write any rule that a computer can check with clear data. Common rules for regulated assets are:

- **Identity (KYC).** Only wallets linked to customers who passed KYC (know your customer) checks can send or receive.
- **Country rules.** The chain blocks transfers to or from countries where the product is not allowed.
- **Blocked addresses.** The chain rejects transfers to addresses on a sanctions list or an internal blocklist.
- **Investor limits.** The chain caps how much one investor can hold or buy, or it allows only qualified investors.
- **Transfer limits.** Each client gets a daily limit and a limit for each transaction.
- **Lock-ups.** The chain stops transfers of a token until a set date.
- **Maker-checker approvals.** One person prepares a large transaction, and a second person approves it.
- **Supply rules.** The chain rejects any mint that puts the supply above the reserve. Our post on [proof of reserve](../proof-of-reserve-explained/) explains this rule.

## Where can the rules run?

Rules can run in four places. Only one of them checks every transaction before it executes.

| Where the rule runs | What it covers | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|
| After the fact, in monitoring | Reports on transactions that already happened | The breach has already happened |
| In the app | Transactions that go through that app | A user can go around the app and send to the chain directly |
| In the token contract | Transfers of that one token | Each token carries its own copy of the rules |
| In the chain, before execution | Every transaction on the chain | Needs a chain built for it |

App checks are the weakest, because the chain accepts transactions from any client software. A token contract (a smart contract that issues and moves one token) is stronger. But each token carries its own copy of the rules, and the copies can drift apart. Rules in the chain apply in the same way to every token, every app and every account. Our comparison of [permissioned and permissionless blockchains](../permissioned-vs-permissionless-blockchain/) explains why this is easier on a permissioned network.

## How does a transaction pass through compliance as code?

Each transaction goes through the same checks, in this order:

1. A client signs a transfer and sends it to the network.
2. The chain finds the rules that apply to the sender, the receiver and the asset.
3. The chain checks each rule: identity status, country, limits, lock-ups and approvals.
4. If one check fails, the chain rejects the transfer. It never executes, and no balance changes.
5. If all checks pass, the transfer executes, and the validators make it final.

Here is an example. A fund token allows only verified investors in approved countries, with a limit of 50,000 units each. An investor who holds 45,000 units tries to buy 10,000 more. The chain rejects the purchase before it executes, because it breaks the limit. The seller keeps the units, the buyer keeps the cash, and nobody needs to unwind anything.

When a trade does pass, [atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/) moves the asset and the payment in one step. Our [asset tokenization guide](../asset-tokenization-guide/) shows where the rules fit in a full launch.

## What are the limits of compliance as code?

Compliance as code is strong, but it has limits. Plan for these five:

- **Data quality.** The code can check only what it knows. If a KYC record is wrong, the check is wrong too.
- **Judgment calls.** Some decisions need a person, for example a review of unusual activity. The code can hold the transaction until a person approves it.
- **Changes in the law.** Rules change over time. Update the code through a controlled process, with tests and a second approver.
- **Privacy.** The rules need identity data, but other parties must not see it. Keep that data encrypted, and share only the result of each check.
- **The full program.** Code enforces rules. People still write the policy, train staff and report to regulators.

## How does Hyper 0X run compliance as code?

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain, checks compliance rules before a transaction executes, not after. Each customer gets a private L2 with its own rules. An L2 is a private blockchain that settles on a main chain. The chain checks limits, KYC status and maker-checker approvals for every transaction on that L2. Our post on [layer 1 and layer 2 blockchains](../layer-1-vs-layer-2-blockchain/) explains how the layers work together.

Consensus on Hyper 0X has no leader, and every validator is a known party with a certificate. Each transaction is final in one pass, with no reorgs (rewrites of recent blocks). So a transaction that passed the rules stays on the record, as our post on [blockchain finality](../blockchain-finality-explained/) explains. Per-party encryption keeps identity data and payments private to the parties. Smart contract upgrades on Hyper 0X need approval, and we recommend the same control for every rule change.

Bridges connect each L2 to EVM chains, Solana and Sui when your rules allow it. Our [custom blockchain services](../../services/custom-blockchains/) turn your policy into rules on your own L2, then run the L2 with you.

## Where should you start?

1. List the rules that every transaction must pass: identity, country, limits and approvals.
2. Mark which rules code can check and which rules need a person.
3. Find the data source for each rule, for example your KYC system.
4. Decide who can change a rule, and who must approve the change.
5. Test the rules on a pilot L2 with real cases, both allowed and blocked.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to turn your compliance rules into code on Hyper 0X.

## What Is MEV and How Can a Wallet Protect Users?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/mev-protection-explained/

MEV, or maximal extractable value, is the profit that someone can take when they choose the order of transactions in a block. On many public blockchains, bots watch pending swaps, trade just before them and sell just after. The user gets a worse price, and the bot keeps the difference. A wallet protects users with tight price limits, hidden order flow and settlement where nobody can trade ahead of an order.

## What is MEV?

A blockchain groups transactions into blocks. Before a transaction enters a block, it waits in a public queue that many chains call the mempool. Anyone can read that queue. The party that builds the next block decides the order of the transactions in it.

That power to set the order is worth money. If you know that a large purchase is coming, you can buy first and sell to the buyer at a higher price. In traditional markets, this is front-running, and the rules forbid brokers to do it with client orders. On many public blockchains, no broker stands in the middle. Bots compete openly for the profit, and the block builder often takes a share.

The term started as "miner extractable value". It now covers every party that orders transactions, such as validators and block builders. A validator is a computer that checks transactions and adds blocks to the chain.

## How does a sandwich attack work?

A sandwich attack is the form of MEV that hurts wallet users most often. A bot places one trade before the swap of the user and one trade after it. The example below uses invented figures.

1. **The user asks for a swap.** Ana swaps $10,000 of stablecoin for a token. She accepts up to 1 percent slippage, that is, a price up to 1 percent worse than the quote.
2. **A bot sees the swap.** The swap waits in the public mempool. A bot reads its size and its slippage limit.
3. **The bot buys first.** The bot pays a higher fee, so its own purchase goes first. That purchase pushes the token price up.
4. **The swap of Ana fills at a worse price.** The new price is close to her limit, but still inside it. Her swap goes through, and she gets about $95 less of the token than the quote showed.
5. **The bot sells.** Right after the swap, the bot sells at the higher price and keeps the difference.

Ana sees a completed swap. She does not see the two trades around it. That is why MEV is a hidden cost.

## What other kinds of MEV are there?

Not all MEV harms users. Some of it keeps prices in line across markets. The table shows the main types.

| Type | What the bot does | Effect on the user |
|---|---|---|
| Front-running | Copies a pending trade and places it first | A worse price |
| Sandwich attack | Trades before and after a pending swap | A worse price, up to the slippage limit |
| Back-running | Trades right after a large swap | Usually no direct harm |
| Arbitrage | Buys where a token is cheap and sells where it is expensive | Keeps prices in line, no direct harm |
| Liquidation | Closes loans that lack enough collateral, for a reward | Harm only to the borrower who loses the position |

Wallet users care most about the first two. Both depend on one condition. A third party can see the swap before it settles and can place trades around it.

## Why does MEV matter to a wallet business?

MEV is a cost that users cannot see but still feel. They compare the quote with the result, and the gap looks like a bad wallet. Users blame the app, not the bot. For a bank or fintech that adds crypto swaps, this is a trust problem and a product problem.

The cost also grows with success. Larger swaps and thin markets attract more bots. A wallet that sends every swap to the public mempool with a wide default slippage gives bots an easy target. If you plan your own wallet, read [how to launch a crypto wallet](../how-to-launch-a-crypto-wallet/) for the full build list.

## How can a wallet protect users from MEV?

No single setting removes MEV. A good wallet combines several layers.

1. **Tight slippage by default.** A smaller limit leaves less room for a sandwich. The wallet sets the limit for the size of the trade and the depth of the market.
2. **Hidden order flow.** The wallet sends the swap straight to the parties that build blocks, not to the public mempool. Bots cannot attack a swap that they cannot see.
3. **Best-route quotes.** The wallet routes the swap across markets for the best price. It shows the minimum amount that the user will get.
4. **Fixed matching rules.** Some venues match orders by rules that every party can check. Nobody can then reorder trades for profit.
5. **Atomic settlement.** Both sides of the trade settle in one step, or neither side settles. Read more in [atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/).
6. **Clear results.** The wallet shows the quote, the fill and the fee side by side, so users see what they paid.

| Topic | Unprotected swap | Protected swap |
|---|---|---|
| Who sees the swap first | Anyone who reads the mempool | Only the parties that settle it |
| Default slippage | Wide, set once | Tight, set per trade |
| Order of trades | Set by whoever builds the block | Set by fixed matching rules |
| If one leg fails | On cross-chain swaps, one leg can settle alone | Both legs settle, or neither |
| What the user sees | A finished swap with a hidden cost | Quote, fill and fee side by side |

## How do Hyper Wallet and Hyper 0X protect swaps?

[Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/) is a non-custodial wallet and exchange in one app. Non-custodial means that the private keys stay on the device of the user. Users sign in with passkeys instead of seed phrases. Each swap in Hyper Wallet has MEV protection. Swaps take the best route, and both sides settle at the same time.

On Hyper 0X, the Buckleson blockchain, the protection goes deeper. A central limit order book runs inside Hyper 0X consensus. A central limit order book is a list of buy and sell orders that the system matches by price and time. Consensus is the process that validators use to agree on the state of the chain. Every validator calculates the same fills, so nobody can trade ahead of an order.

Users also pay one fee, not two. They pay one transaction cost, with no exchange fee and wallet fee on top. Banks and fintechs can put Hyper Wallet into their own app with the Hyper Wallet SDKs. See [what a wallet SDK is](../what-is-a-wallet-sdk/) for how that works.

## What does MEV protection not cover?

MEV protection stops other parties from trading around a swap. It does not protect users from every loss.

- **Normal price moves.** The price changes between the quote and the fill when the market moves.
- **Thin markets.** A large swap in a small market moves the price on its own.
- **Bad tokens.** Protection does not make a scam token safe to buy.
- **Phishing.** A fake site can still trick a user into signing a bad transaction.

Good wallet design handles these with clear warnings, token checks and signing screens that show exactly what the user approves. Who holds the keys also matters here, as [custodial vs non-custodial wallets](../custodial-vs-non-custodial-wallet/) explains.

## Where should you start?

1. Measure the gap between the quote and the fill on your current swaps.
2. Set a tight default slippage, and adjust it to trade size and market depth.
3. Keep swaps out of the public mempool where the chain allows it.
4. Settle trades atomically, so no user holds only one side of a trade.
5. Show the quote, the fill and the fee on every swap screen.
6. Choose a wallet stack with MEV protection built in, such as the Hyper Wallet SDKs.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to review how your swaps fill today.

## MPC vs Multisig Wallets: Which Is Safer?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/mpc-vs-multisig-wallets/

Neither model is safer in every case. An MPC wallet splits one private key into shares that sign together, so the full key never exists in one place. A multisig wallet uses several full keys, and a set number of them must sign each transaction. Both remove the single point of failure of a one-key wallet. The safer choice depends on who holds the shares or keys, how you recover access and how you approve transfers.

## What is an MPC wallet?

A private key is the secret number that signs transactions. Whoever holds it controls the funds. MPC, or multi-party computation, lets several parties compute a result together without any party seeing the inputs of the others. An MPC wallet uses it to create and use a key that no single party ever holds.

The shares sit on different devices, for example a phone, a server and a backup. To sign, a set number of shares, such as two of three, run a joint process. The output is one normal signature. The blockchain sees an ordinary wallet and cannot tell that several parties signed.

You can also refresh the shares. The parties create new shares for the same key, and the old shares stop working. The wallet address does not change.

## What is a multisig wallet?

A multisig (multi-signature) wallet uses several separate private keys. Each signer holds one full key. A rule on the chain says how many signatures a transaction needs, for example two of three. On some chains this rule is part of the chain itself. On others, a smart contract (a program on the blockchain) applies it.

Because the rule lives on the chain, anyone can check it. The record shows which keys signed each transaction. To add or remove a signer, the current signers approve a change on the chain. On some chains, that change means a new wallet address.

## How do MPC and multisig wallets compare?

The table compares the two models side by side.

| Topic | MPC wallet | Multisig wallet |
|---|---|---|
| How control splits | One key, split into shares | Several full keys |
| What the chain sees | One normal signature | Several signatures or a contract call |
| Where the approval rule lives | In the signing software, off the chain | On the chain, open to anyone |
| Chain support | Any chain with a supported signature type | Only chains with multisig or smart contracts |
| Network fees | The same as a single-key wallet | Often higher, because of the extra checks |
| Change of signers | Refresh the shares, same address | A transaction on the chain, sometimes a new address |
| Record of who signed | In the logs of the provider | On the chain, for each transaction |
| Main weak point | The signing software and who holds the shares | The key storage of each signer and contract bugs |

## Which model is safer against theft?

Both models stop a thief who takes one key or one share. The real question is who can reach enough shares or keys to sign. If a provider holds two of three MPC shares, it can move funds alone. Then the wallet is custodial in practice, as our post on [custodial vs non-custodial wallets](../custodial-vs-non-custodial-wallet/) explains.

Two risks remain in both models. First, signers can collude. Signers who share one laptop give little more protection than one signer. Second, people still approve what they see, and a fake invoice or a fake signing screen can trick them. So the strongest setups also check the transfer itself, not only the number of signatures.

Each model also has its own risk. A bug in MPC signing software can leak shares. A bug in a multisig contract can lock or expose the funds. Choose software with independent security reviews.

## How does recovery work in each model?

The two models recover access in different ways.

1. **MPC.** If a user loses the phone with one share, the other shares still give access. The parties refresh the shares onto a new device, and the old share stops working.
2. **Multisig.** If a signer loses a key, the other signers approve a change that adds a new key. This works only while enough signers can still sign.
3. **Both.** If too many shares or keys go missing at the same time, nobody can move the funds again. Keep backups in separate places, and test recovery before you hold real money.

## How do passkey wallets compare?

A passkey wallet keeps one key on the device of the user, inside the secure chip of the phone. A face scan or a fingerprint gives access to it. With account abstraction, the account itself is a smart contract with its own rules. The rules can set spending limits, add a second device and let an app pay the network fees. Recovery is part of the account design, so a lost phone is not a lost wallet.

Passkey wallets solve a different problem. MPC and multisig split control among several people or devices. A passkey wallet makes the control of one person simple and safe. A smart account can also combine both ideas: a passkey for daily use and a second approval for large transfers. Read [account abstraction without seed phrases](../account-abstraction-no-seed-phrases/) for the full model.

## Which teams fit which model?

Match the model to who holds the money and who approves a transfer.

- **Consumer apps and neobanks.** Use passkey wallets with account abstraction, so users sign with a face scan and keep their own keys.
- **Fintechs that run wallets on many chains.** MPC fits well, because one setup works on every chain with a supported signature type.
- **Treasuries and funds on one chain.** Multisig fits well when the board wants every approval on the public record.
- **Banks and regulated custodians.** Use maker-checker approvals, where one person proposes a transfer and a second person approves it. MPC or keys in a hardware security module (HSM) both work here.

## What does this look like for a fintech?

Take a fintech with a retail app and a made-up $5M treasury. Retail users get passkey wallets, with the keys on their phones. The treasury needs two people for every transfer. The fintech picks a two-of-three setup: the finance lead, the treasury officer and a backup in a safe.

One day, the treasury officer loses a laptop. With MPC, the team refreshes the shares, and the share on the laptop stops working. With multisig, the finance lead and the backup approve a change that replaces the lost key. In both cases the treasury stays safe, because one share or one key cannot sign alone.

## How does Hyper 0X handle wallet keys and approvals?

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain, puts approval rules on the chain. It runs compliance as code: the chain checks limits, KYC and maker-checker approvals before a transaction executes. So a large or unusual transfer waits for a second person. With account abstraction, users sign in with a face scan or a passkey, not a seed phrase.

[Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/) is under development as a non-custodial wallet and exchange in one app. Non-custodial means that the private keys stay on the device of the user. It will run on many chains. Banks and fintechs will use the Hyper Wallet SDKs to launch their own wallet, neobank or payment gateway on Hyper 0X. A business that needs custody will add it through the SDKs. See [what a wallet SDK is](../what-is-a-wallet-sdk/) for how SDKs work.

Our [wallet and exchange services](../../services/wallets-exchanges/) build the same kind of wallet for you, with no seed phrases, maker-checker approvals and compliance as code. For build versus white-label, read [how to launch a crypto wallet](../how-to-launch-a-crypto-wallet/).

## Where should you start?

1. List every wallet that you run, the funds in each and who can move them.
2. Decide who must approve each type of transfer, and write the rule down.
3. Pick the key model for each wallet: passkeys for users, MPC or multisig for shared funds.
4. Check who holds enough shares or keys to sign alone.
5. Put limits and maker-checker approvals into code that runs before each transfer.
6. Test recovery for a lost device and for a signer who leaves, before you go live.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to choose the right wallet model for your team.

## What Is Proof of Reserve for Tokenized Assets?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/proof-of-reserve-explained/

Proof of reserve is evidence that the real assets behind a token exist and are at least equal to the tokens in circulation. It compares two numbers: the token supply on the blockchain and the assets that a custodian holds. When the reserve is equal to or larger than the supply, every token has full backing. The strongest proof of reserve is frequent, independent and linked to the rule that mints new tokens.

## Why does proof of reserve matter?

A tokenized asset is only as good as the asset behind it. A token for gold, a fund unit or a bond is a claim on something real. The holder trusts that the issuer holds that asset and keeps it safe. If the reserve is short, the last holders to redeem can lose money. In past failures of crypto platforms, customers learned about a shortfall only after withdrawals stopped.

For executives, proof of reserve is a trust tool and a sales tool. Investors, partners and regulators ask for it before they commit money. A clear reserve record also shortens due diligence, because a buyer can check the backing directly. Our [asset tokenization guide](../asset-tokenization-guide/) puts proof of reserve in the first step of a launch: structure and custody.

## What does proof of reserve compare?

Proof of reserve compares what the issuer owes with what the issuer holds. The two halves need different checks.

- **Liabilities (the tokens).** Every token is a claim on the reserve. On a blockchain (a shared ledger that many computers keep in sync), you can count the tokens in circulation at any moment. This half of the check is exact and live.
- **Assets (the reserve).** The real asset stays off the chain with a custodian, a regulated firm that holds assets for others. A vault, a bank or a fund administrator reports what it holds. This half needs an independent check.

The reserve ratio is the reserve divided by the supply. A ratio of 1.0 or more means full backing. Say that an issuer has minted 100,000 gold tokens of one gram each. The vault must then hold at least 100 kg of gold for the token holders.

## What are the main methods of proof of reserve?

Issuers use five main methods. Most strong programs combine two or more of them.

| Method | What it shows | How often | Main limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attestation | An accounting firm confirms that the reserve covered the supply on one date | Monthly or quarterly | A snapshot of one day |
| Full audit | The controls and finances of the issuer over a period | Usually yearly | Slow, and less common |
| Holdings report | Each asset in the reserve, for example each gold bar with its serial number | With each attestation | The custodian prepares it |
| On-chain reserve feed | The reserve figure on the blockchain, next to the live supply | With each update | Only as good as its data source |
| Holder balance proof | Each holder can check that their balance is in the total | With each report | Shows what is owed, not what is held |

An attestation is the most common method today. An accounting firm checks the records of the custodian on one date and confirms the totals. A full audit goes deeper and tests the controls of the issuer over a full period. An on-chain reserve feed puts the reserve figure on the blockchain. There, a smart contract (a program on the blockchain) can read it and act on it.

## Where does proof of reserve fall short?

Proof of reserve answers one question: does the asset exist? It does not answer every question about the issuer. Watch for these gaps.

- **Snapshots.** A report on one date says nothing about the other days. An issuer can borrow assets for the check and return them the next day.
- **Hidden claims.** The reserve can exist and also secure a loan. Ask whether any other party has a claim on the assets.
- **Quality of the reserve.** Cash, short-term government bonds and corporate debt carry different risks. A full ratio in weak assets is not the same as a full ratio in cash.
- **The data source.** An on-chain feed is only as accurate as the custodian report behind it. An independent firm must still check the custodian.
- **The legal claim.** Holders need a legal right to the reserve if the issuer fails. A trust or a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) keeps the assets away from the creditors of the issuer.

When you read a reserve report, check five things. Check the date, the firm and the scope. Check the ratio and the type of assets. Then compare the report with the live supply on the chain.

## How do you build proof of reserve into a tokenized asset?

Build proof of reserve into the mint rule, not only into a report. A report finds a gap after it happens. A mint rule stops the gap before it starts. Do these steps in this order:

1. **Hold the asset with an independent custodian.** Keep allocated, segregated holdings in a trust or an SPV.
2. **Mint one to one.** Create tokens only when matching assets arrive in custody. Burn (destroy) tokens when assets leave.
3. **Put the reserve figure on the chain.** The custodian signs each reserve update with its own key.
4. **Make the mint check the reserve.** Write a rule that rejects any mint that puts the supply above the reserve.
5. **Keep independent checks.** Publish regular attestations, because the feed only repeats what the custodian reports.
6. **Watch the ratio.** Alert the issuer and pause new mints when the ratio falls below 1.0.

Our post on [tokenized gold](../tokenized-gold-explained/) shows how bar lists and attestations work for one asset class. The same steps apply to fund units, bonds and invoices.

## How does Hyper 0X support proof of reserve?

On [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain, each issuer runs its own private L2. An L2 is a private blockchain that settles on a main chain. Hyper 0X runs compliance as code: rules that the chain checks before a transaction executes. You can write the mint limit from step 4 as one of these rules. A mint that exceeds the signed reserve figure fails, and it never reaches the ledger.

Hyper 0X is final in one pass, with no reorgs (rewrites of recent blocks). So the supply that an auditor reads today is the same supply tomorrow. Our post on [blockchain finality](../blockchain-finality-explained/) explains why this matters. Per-party encryption keeps the records of each investor private. The issuer can still give an auditor access to the supply and the reserve record.

Trades also stay clean. When an investor buys or sells a token for cash, both legs settle in one step through [atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/). No investor pays without the token, and no seller delivers without payment. Read [what compliance as code is](../compliance-as-code-blockchain/) for the full rule model. Our [asset tokenization services](../../services/asset-tokenization/) build the token, the reserve checks, the investor rules and the app as one system.

## Where should you start?

1. Write down the asset, the custodian and the legal structure that holds the asset.
2. Decide how often you will publish reserve data, and which firm will check it.
3. Ask the custodian if it can sign reserve updates and send them to the chain.
4. Write the mint rule: no new tokens above the reserve.
5. Show the reserve ratio where investors can see it at any time.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to design proof of reserve for your tokenized asset.
