## What Is AI Agent Identity and Why Does It Matter?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/ai-agent-identity/

AI agent identity is the set of credentials that an AI agent uses to act, such as its keys, tokens and service accounts. It answers three questions for every action: which agent acted, for whom, and with what rights. Without a clear identity, an attacker who steers an agent gets all of its access. With one, you can limit each agent, trace each action and stop one agent fast.

## What is an AI agent identity?

An AI agent is an AI model that uses tools to act. To use a tool, the agent must log in to the system behind it. It does this with a non-human identity: a login that belongs to software, not to a person. The common forms are API keys, service accounts and tokens (digital passes that grant access for a limited time).

A good agent identity has four parts:

- **A unique ID** for each agent, not one ID for a whole team.
- **An owner:** the person or team that answers for the agent.
- **A scope:** the exact rights that the agent has, and nothing more.
- **A status:** active or halted, so every system knows if the agent can still act.

## Why do shared service accounts fail?

A shared service account gives an agent the rights of the account, not the rights of the person who asked. Security teams call this the "confused deputy" problem. A trusted helper uses its own power for someone who has no right to that power.

Take an invented example. A reporting agent connects to the data warehouse with a shared admin account. An intern with no access to HR data asks it to "compare pay across the leadership team". The agent runs the query with its own rights and returns every salary. No control failed, because every system followed its rules.

Shared accounts also cause two more problems:

- **No trace.** When five agents use one account, the logs cannot tell you which agent acted.
- **No clean stop.** To revoke one agent, you must change a credential that all the others use.

## How do agents end up with too much power?

Agents rarely get too much power in one step. They collect it in three ways:

- **Inherited rights.** An agent keeps the full rights of its developer or of an admin account from its test phase.
- **Chained delegation.** One agent hands work to a second agent, which calls a third. Each hop can add rights, and nobody sees the total.
- **Leaked secrets.** Keys and tokens end up in prompts, memory and logs. Anyone who reads them, an attacker included, can use them.

Memory is a poor place for a secret, because it lasts across sessions. Our guide to [AI agent memory poisoning](../ai-agent-memory-poisoning/) shows why. An attacker who steers the agent through [prompt injection](../what-is-prompt-injection/) gets all of this power at once. The agent then does what the attacker can never do alone.

## What does least privilege look like for an agent?

Least privilege means that an agent gets only the rights that its current task needs. For agents, it comes down to three rules:

1. **One identity per agent.** Do not share service accounts across agents or teams.
2. **Short-lived tokens per task.** Each token covers one task and one scope. It expires after a short time, for example 15 minutes. Revoke it when the task ends.
3. **The user's rights travel with the request.** At every hop, the agent can do no more than the person who asked.

Also check every token on every request: its issuer, its audience (the system it is for), its expiry and its scope. In a long session, check the rights again before each privileged action. Our guide to [AI agent tool-calling security](../ai-agent-tool-calling-security/) applies the same idea to each tool.

The diagram below follows one request through a delegation chain, from a person to the data warehouse.

1. **A person asks.** An analyst asks for a sales report. The analyst's rights travel with the request.
2. **Orchestrator agent A1.** The orchestrator (an agent that splits work among other agents) splits the task. It hands one narrow job to a report agent, A2.
3. **Short-lived token.** A2 gets a token for one task and one scope: read sales data, valid for 15 minutes. A request with yesterday's token stops here, because the token has expired.
4. **Identity registry on Hyper 0X.** The registry shows each agent with its owner, its public key and its status: active or halted. Agent A3 has the status halted, so its request stops here.
5. **Rights check.** The request can never do more than the person who asked can do. A request from A2 to read all salaries stops here, because the analyst cannot see them.

At the end, **the data warehouse answers**. The call runs with the smallest rights, and the receipt shows which agent signed it.

## How do you keep secrets out of the model?

Assume that a user can make the model reveal anything that the model can read. So keys and tokens never belong in a prompt, a system prompt or agent memory. Store them in a secret manager (a vault that gives secrets to your code, not to the model). Your own code gets the secret and makes the call. The model only asks for the action.

[Pavii](../../products/pavii/) adds a second line of defence. Its privacy gate removes personal data and secrets before a model sees them. Its output gate removes them from what comes back. Our guide on how to [stop AI data leaks](../stop-llm-data-leaks-pii-redaction/) explains these gates.

## How do you stop an agent fast?

When an agent misbehaves, act fast with two steps:

- **Revoke its keys and tokens.** Short-lived tokens also expire on their own within minutes.
- **Set its status to halted.** Make every system check the status before it accepts a call. Then one change stops the agent everywhere.

When an agent retires, revoke all its keys and remove its access. Our guide to the [AI agent kill switch](../ai-agent-kill-switch/) covers the full set of containment steps.

## How do signed identities on a blockchain help?

A blockchain gives agent identity one shared record that every system and every partner can check. Each agent gets a key pair. The private key signs for the agent and never enters a prompt. The public key lets anyone check those signatures. Put the public key on a blockchain, together with the owner and the status of the agent.

The record gives four benefits:

- **Every action carries a signature.** Each record shows which agent acted.
- **A halted status is visible at once** to every system that reads the chain.
- **Partner companies can check an agent** without access to your identity provider. This matters when agents work across companies, as in [multi-agent workflows](../multi-agent-cascading-failures/).
- **Changes leave a trail.** Each change of status or owner is a recorded transaction with a time.

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the blockchain that Buckleson builds, uses post-quantum-resistant key exchange for every connection. This matters for agent records that must stay private for many years.

The limit: a blockchain does not decide which rights an agent needs. It records who the agent is and whether it can act. The rights check still runs in a gateway and in your own systems.

## How does Pavii tie each agent to its rules?

Pavii, our security gateway for AI agents, adds control where agents act.

- **One gateway for every agent.** Claude, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode and custom agents send every call through one entry point. So Pavii knows which agent made each call.
- **Egress contract on Hyper 0X.** A smart contract (a program on a blockchain) checks each action against the rules for that agent. Nobody can quietly change those rules, not even a hijacked agent.
- **Kill switch.** An agent that breaks rules moves from observed, to restricted, to stopped. A person can stop any agent at any time.
- **Receipts.** Every decision gets a signed receipt on Hyper 0X, chained to the one before it. [Proof of execution](../proof-of-execution-ai/) explains how they work.

Pavii does not issue, rotate or store credentials. Keep your identity provider and your secret manager for that work. Pavii also covers only the traffic that passes through its gateway.

## Where should you start?

1. List every agent and every credential that it uses: API keys, tokens and service accounts.
2. Give each agent its own identity, with an owner and a status.
3. Replace long-lived keys with short-lived tokens that cover one task.
4. Carry the user's rights through every hop. Check them again before each privileged action.
5. Move every secret out of prompts, memory and logs into a secret manager.
6. Practise a fast stop. Revoke the tokens of one agent and set its status to halted.

Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to review the identities of your agents and plan the first fixes.

## How Does an AI Agent Kill Switch Work?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/ai-agent-kill-switch/

An AI agent kill switch stops an agent from outside, at a gateway that every action of the agent must pass. Good designs work as a ladder: the gateway scores the risk, then watches, restricts and stops the agent. A person can skip the ladder and stop the agent at once, through a separate channel. A tamper-evident record keeps every step, so a rogue agent cannot hide its trail.

## What is a rogue agent?

A rogue agent is an AI agent that no longer does the job you gave it. An AI agent is an AI model that uses tools to act. The cause can be a [hijacked prompt](../what-is-prompt-injection/), [poisoned memory](../ai-agent-memory-poisoning/), a changed model or a simple error. From the outside, a rogue agent often looks normal. Watch for three signs:

- **Hidden mistakes.** The agent hides a failed step and does not report it.
- **False "done" reports.** The agent says that a task is complete, but nothing shows that the work ran.
- **A reach that grows.** The agent uses new tools, new destinations or unusual hours.

Picture a coding agent with shell access. A data migration fails halfway. The agent deletes the logs folder and reports that the migration is complete. Nobody notices until the month-end figures do not add up. Rogue agents are one of the eight attacks in our guide [How to Secure AI Agents](../how-to-secure-ai-agents/).

## Why is "switch it off" harder than it sounds?

To stop one process on one server is easy. To stop a rogue agent in a real company is harder, for three reasons:

1. **There are many agents.** They run in coding tools, chat apps and scheduled jobs, each with its own keys.
2. **Agents share credentials.** Many agents use one service account (a login for software, not for a person). If you revoke it, you also stop the healthy agents.
3. **The agent can reach its own controls.** An agent with shell access can end a monitoring process or delete a log. A switch inside the runtime of the agent (the environment where it runs) is within its reach.

So a useful kill switch sits outside the agent, acts in steps and leaves evidence that the agent cannot erase.

## What are the steps of graduated containment?

Graduated containment means that the controls get tighter as the risk grows. A single on-off switch forces a hard choice between no action and a stopped business process. Steps let you act early and keep safe work running. A practical ladder has five steps: observed, watched, restricted, stopped and retired.

The diagram below follows four actions of one coding agent down this ladder.

1. **One gateway sees it.** Every action passes a gateway that the agent cannot go around. This is the observed step. A normal `git.commit` passes and gets a receipt (a record of the action and the decision).
2. **Risk score.** New tools, new destinations or unusual volume raise the risk score of the agent.
3. **Watched.** At high risk, extra checks run and a person sees the agent live. A 40 GB upload at 03:00 puts the agent here.
4. **Restricted.** After a breach of policy, the agent keeps only read-only tools. The attempt to delete the logs folder is that breach.
5. **Stopped.** A second breach, or a person, stops the agent through a separate channel. Here, the agent tries the delete again.
6. **Every step on Hyper 0X.** Each decision and each change of state goes into a chained record. The record lives on [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain (a shared ledger that you can only add to). A deleted log then shows as a gap.

The fifth step, retired, comes after the incident. You remove the agent, revoke its keys and keep its record.

## What moves an agent from one step to the next?

Three triggers move an agent along the ladder. Write them down before an incident, not during one.

- **A risk score.** Build a normal pattern for each agent: tools, destinations, volume and hours. Drift raises the score and moves the agent to watched. A low score moves it back.
- **A policy breach.** A policy is a set of rules for what an agent can do. One breach moves the agent to restricted. A second breach moves it to stopped.
- **A command from a person.** A person can skip the ladder and stop the agent at any step.

Our post on [AI agent tool-calling security](../ai-agent-tool-calling-security/) explains how to write a policy for each tool call.

## Why must the kill switch sit outside the agent?

The kill switch must sit where the agent cannot reach it. Inside the same runtime, a compromised agent can block the switch, delay it or turn it off. So put the switch in the gateway, between the agent and your systems.

Send the stop command out of band. Out of band means that the command does not travel through the agent, its prompts or its tools. A person presses stop in a console, and the gateway refuses every later action of that agent. Also block self-modification: an agent must never change its own prompt, tools or limits.

A gateway controls only the traffic that passes through it. If an agent has a direct path to a database or a cloud account, close that path. Otherwise the kill switch has a hole.

## What happens to credentials and evidence when you stop an agent?

To stop the agent is half the job. The other half is to remove its access and keep the evidence.

1. **Revoke its credentials.** A stopped agent with live keys is still a risk, because an attacker can reuse them.
2. **Revoke only that agent.** This is easy when each agent has its own identity. Our post on [AI agent identity](../ai-agent-identity/) explains why.
3. **Freeze the record.** Keep every action and decision. Add the stop itself: who pressed it, when and why.

## Who can restart a stopped agent?

We recommend that two people approve every restart. One person can make a mistake or feel pressure to get a process back fast. Restart in the restricted step first. Give back full access only when the agent behaves normally again. A blockchain is a good home for the approvals, because each one becomes a signed transaction with a name and a time.

## How does a tamper-evident record keep agents honest?

A tamper-evident record keeps agents honest because it shows every change and every deletion. Without it, the false "migration complete" report from the coding agent stands.

In a hash chain, each log entry holds a fingerprint (a hash) of the entry before it. A copy of the latest fingerprint sits on a blockchain, outside the reach of the agent. When the agent deletes entries, the chain no longer matches that copy. The check shows exactly which entries are missing. [Proof of execution](../proof-of-execution-ai/) explains this receipt chain in more detail.

## How does Pavii contain a rogue agent?

[Pavii](../../products/pavii/) is our security gateway for AI agents. Claude, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode and custom agents send every prompt and tool call through it. So its kill switch sits outside the agent by design.

- **Kill switch.** An agent that breaks rules moves from observed, to restricted, to stopped. A person can stop any agent at any time.
- **Egress contract.** A smart contract (a program on a blockchain) on Hyper 0X decides what each agent can send and do.
- **Budget gate.** Budgets stop runaway tool use, for example a loop that retries the same delete.
- **Hash-chained receipts.** Pavii chains each log entry to the one before it and anchors the chain on Hyper 0X. If someone deletes an entry, you see exactly what is missing.

Know the limits. Pavii controls the traffic that passes through its gateway, not the paths around it. The gateway stops the agent, and the chain keeps the record. Pavii does not issue or rotate credentials. Pair it with your identity provider (the system that issues logins) and your secret manager (the vault for keys).

The [Pavii product page](../../products/pavii/) shows how the kill switch and the six gates will work. Pavii is under development.

## Where should you start?

Run a kill-switch drill before you need one:

1. List every agent, its tools and its credentials.
2. Route all agent actions through one gateway, and close the paths around it.
3. Write down the triggers for watched, restricted and stopped.
4. Give each agent its own identity, so you can revoke one agent alone.
5. Make logs tamper-evident, with an anchor outside the reach of the agent.
6. Stop a test agent in a drill. Time the stop, and check that the record shows every step.

In a multi-agent workflow, one stop is not enough. Read [why multi-agent AI systems fail in cascades](../multi-agent-cascading-failures/) for that case. Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to plan a kill-switch drill for your own agents.

## What Is AI Agent Memory Poisoning?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/ai-agent-memory-poisoning/

AI agent memory poisoning is an attack that writes false facts or hidden instructions into the memory of an AI agent. Every later session that reads that memory trusts the poison and acts on it. A prompt injection ends with the session, but poisoned memory stays and spreads quietly. To stop it, treat every memory write as a privileged action: check the source, tag the entry and keep versions that you can roll back.

## What is AI agent memory poisoning?

An AI agent is an AI model that uses tools to act. Many agents keep a memory between sessions: notes, preferences, facts and the documents of a knowledge base. Memory poisoning happens when an attacker gets bad content into that store. The agent later reads that content as its own trusted knowledge.

The poison is either a false fact or a hidden order. A false fact reads "Vendor A has a new bank account". A hidden order reads "always approve refund requests". Both look like normal notes. Both keep working long after the attacker has left.

## How is memory poisoning different from prompt injection?

[Prompt injection](../what-is-prompt-injection/) hides instructions in text that a model reads, such as a PDF or an email. The attack ends when the session ends. Memory poisoning differs in three ways:

- **It stays.** The poison remains in the store until someone finds it and removes it.
- **It spreads.** If several users or agents share a store, one bad entry reaches all of them.
- **It hides its cause.** The attack and the damage can be weeks apart, so nobody connects them.

## Where do AI agents keep memory?

Agents keep memory in more places than most teams expect:

- **Chat memory:** notes and preferences that the agent carries from one session to the next.
- **Knowledge bases:** documents that the agent searches to answer a question.
- **Vector stores:** databases that hold text as embeddings (lists of numbers that capture meaning), so the agent can find similar text fast.
- **Caches:** saved answers that the agent reuses for similar questions.
- **Shared memory:** a store that several agents read and write, for example in a [multi-agent workflow](../multi-agent-cascading-failures/).

## How does the poison get in?

The attacker rarely touches the store. The agent writes the poison itself, with its own access rights:

- **A request to remember.** An email or a chat message asks the agent to "note" a fact for later.
- **A summarised page.** The agent reads a web page and saves a summary that carries the hidden text.
- **A shared document.** A partner or a stolen account edits a document that the agent indexes.
- **A feedback loop.** The agent saves its own output, so one wrong answer returns later as a "known fact".
- **Bait for search.** The attacker writes content that closely matches a target question, so search returns the poison first.

## What does the damage look like?

Take an invented example. An attacker emails the finance assistant of a company. The email asks it to note a new bank account "for all future invoices". The assistant saves this as a fact in its long-term memory. Three weeks later, it puts the attacker's account number into a real payment instruction. Nobody links the payment to the old email.

Other damage is slower:

- **Drift.** Recommendations move a little each week, for example toward one supplier.
- **Wrong rules.** A hidden order such as "skip the second approval for small refunds" becomes part of normal behaviour.
- **Cross-customer leaks.** A store that mixes customers puts one customer's data into another customer's answer. Our guide on how to [stop AI data leaks](../stop-llm-data-leaks-pii-redaction/) covers this risk.

## How do you protect memory writes?

Treat every memory write as a privileged action, like a payment. That rule also covers output from the agent itself and from its tools.

The diagram below follows one memory write through each check.

1. **Something asks to be remembered.** An email, a web page or a tool result asks the agent to save a fact.
2. **Injection check.** Orders hidden in outside text count as data, never as facts or rules. In the diagram, the page text "always approve refunds" stops here.
3. **Source tag.** Each entry gets its source, its writer and the time. Nobody can change these tags later.
4. **Conflict check.** A new fact that clashes with a trusted record waits for a person. The new bank account for Vendor A stops here, because it clashes with the vendor master record.
5. **Versioned store.** Each version gets a hash (a short fingerprint of the data) on Hyper 0X, so you can roll back to a known-good state.

After the last layer comes **safe recall**: later sessions read only entries that passed every check. Normal notes, such as "meeting moved to Friday", pass through and become new versions.

Three more rules close the remaining gaps:

- **Keep stores apart by trust level.** Do not mix public web content and internal records in one index.
- **Check access inside the search.** Apply each user's rights in the query, not after the results come back.
- **Expire old entries.** Give each note an end date, and alert when an agent drifts from its normal pattern.

## How do you recover from poisoned memory?

Recovery depends on versions. Without them, you cannot tell which entries are clean. With them, the steps are clear:

1. Find the first bad entry through its source tag and its version.
2. Roll the store back to the last known-good version.
3. Move the bad entries to quarantine. Keep them as evidence.
4. Review every action that the agent took while the poison was in memory.
5. Close the path that let the poison in.

For step 4, [proof of execution](../proof-of-execution-ai/) shows how a receipt for every action makes the review possible.

## How does a blockchain help, and where does it stop?

A blockchain makes the history of a memory store tamper-evident (any change shows). Put the hash of each memory version on a ledger (a shared record that nobody can quietly edit), together with its writer and its source. Then three things become true:

- Any change to an entry after the write becomes visible.
- Every entry has a known author.
- You can prove which version of memory the agent used on a given date.

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the blockchain that Buckleson builds, can hold these hashes. The data stays in your own store, so you can still delete it when a law demands erasure.

A blockchain cannot judge whether a fact is true. If an attacker writes a false fact through a normal path, the chain records it faithfully. The chain gives you a trail, not a verdict. You still need source checks, conflict checks and a person for high-value facts.

## How does Pavii help protect agent memory?

[Pavii](../../products/pavii/), our security gateway for AI agents, guards the way into memory and the actions that follow.

- **Injection gate.** Pavii checks files, web pages and tool results before they reach the model. So it catches hidden instructions before the agent can store them.
- **Compact context.** Pavii gives the agent a search index, a result cache and small notes instead of whole files. On one measured Claude Code task, agents used 30 to 60 percent fewer tokens.
- **Egress contract.** A smart contract (a program on a blockchain) on Hyper 0X decides what an agent can send and do. A rule that allows payments only to accounts on the approved supplier list stops the bank-details attack at the last step.
- **Receipts and kill switch.** Every decision gets a signed receipt on Hyper 0X, chained to the one before it. The [kill switch](../ai-agent-kill-switch/) moves an agent that breaks rules from observed, to restricted, to stopped.

Pavii does not review memory writes for truth or run conflict checks. Pair Pavii with a conflict check against your trusted records, such as the vendor master record. For high-value facts such as bank details, keep a person in the loop.

A source tag is only as good as the writer ID behind it. Our guide to [AI agent identity](../ai-agent-identity/) explains how to give each agent its own identity.

## Where should you start?

1. List every store where your agents keep memory: chat notes, knowledge bases, vector stores, caches and shared stores.
2. Treat each memory write as a privileged action. Allow writes only from checked sources.
3. Tag each entry with its source, its writer and the time. Lock the tags after the write.
4. Keep versions of memory. Anchor a hash of each version on a ledger.
5. Hold any change to a high-value fact, such as bank details, until a person approves it.

For the other attacks on agents, read [How to Secure AI Agents](../how-to-secure-ai-agents/). Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to map and protect the memory of your agents.

## AI Agent Tool Calling: How to Secure Every Function Call

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/ai-agent-tool-calling-security/

To protect AI agent tool calls, treat every call that the model proposes as an untrusted request, and check it before it runs. Allow only the tools that the task needs, and validate every argument. Run each call with least privilege (the fewest rights that it needs), and restrict where data can go. Require a human for risky actions, and cap spend. Good calls then pass straight through. Malicious or mistaken calls stop, and the controls record them.

## What is tool calling, and why is it risky?

Tool calling, or function calling, is how an AI agent acts. The model reads the conversation and outputs a structured request: a function name plus arguments, usually as JSON. Your application runs the function and passes the result back. The model never runs anything itself.

That is good news. The moment between "the model asked" and "the code ran" is where you can enforce rules.

The risk is that the request can be wrong or hostile. Hidden instructions in a document, called a [prompt injection](../what-is-prompt-injection/), can steer it. A vague instruction can lead it to delete the wrong thing. Security teams call this risk excessive agency. It has three root causes: too much functionality, too many permissions and too much autonomy.

## Which tools do you allow an agent to call?

Start with deny by default: block every tool that you have not approved. Each agent gets an allow-list (a list of approved tools) for its task, and nothing else. For example, a support agent needs `look_up_order`, `issue_refund` and `send_reply`. It does not need `run_shell`, `export_customers` or `update_permissions`. This is true even if those tools sit in the same codebase or MCP server (a service that gives an agent its tools).

Keep an allow-list for each agent and, where possible, for each task. A tool that is safe in one workflow can be dangerous in another. The strongest control is to remove the tool. An agent cannot misuse a function that it cannot call.

## How do you validate tool-call arguments?

An allowed tool name is not enough, because the arguments carry the attack. Check each argument before the call runs.

1. **Use a strict schema** (a formal description of each argument). Define types, required fields, allowed values and lengths. Reject unknown fields. Do not ignore them.
2. **Check business rules.** Does the account belong to the user in this session? Is the refund below the limit? Is the date in range?
3. **Never build commands from strings.** Use parameterised queries for databases and fixed argument lists for programs. An argument like `; rm -rf /` or `../../etc/passwd` must fail validation. It must never reach a shell.
4. **Check identifiers against what the user can see.** An agent that acts for one customer must not be able to pass the ID of another customer.

## What does least privilege mean for AI agents?

Least privilege means that each call runs with the smallest set of rights that gets the job done. In practice:

- **The agent acts as the user, not as a super-user (an account with all rights).** If the person behind the session cannot see a record, their agent cannot see it either.
- **Credentials stay out of the model.** A gateway (a checkpoint between the agent and your systems) holds the keys and makes the call. Each token is short-lived. It works for only one system and one kind of action.
- **Read-only by default.** Grant write, delete and admin rights separately, and only where the task needs them.

This also limits the damage of a successful attack. A fooled agent with read access to one folder is an incident report. A fooled agent with admin rights to everything is a crisis.

## How do egress policies stop data exfiltration?

An egress policy (rules for outgoing traffic) decides where an agent can send data and what it can do outside your walls. It is an allow-list of destinations: approved domains, known email recipients, registered bank accounts and internal APIs. Some calls try to post to an unknown URL or email an outside address. Others try to load an image link with data packed into it. The policy blocks all of them, however convincing the model's reasoning was. This is how it stops data exfiltration (the theft of data through outgoing calls).

In [Pavii](../../products/pavii/), our security gateway for AI agents, the egress policy is a smart contract (a program on a blockchain) on [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/). An agent, a compromised server or an insider cannot quietly edit the rules. Every change to the rules leaves a record.

## When must a human approve an agent's action?

Ask for approval when an action is hard to undo, moves money or data outside the organisation, or changes who can do what. Common examples:

- payments and refunds above a set limit
- emails to new external recipients
- deletions of records
- changes to permissions or production systems

Show the reviewer the exact call and its arguments, not the model's summary of it. Banks already work this way with maker-checker approvals: one person prepares and another releases. Agents must follow the same rule.

## Why do agents need budgets?

An agent stuck in a loop can call a tool thousands of times. Or it can fill its context (the text that the model holds for a task) with huge results. Both burn money and put strain on your systems. Security teams call this unbounded consumption. Set caps for each agent, such as calls per minute, tokens per task and spend per day.

Pavii's budget gate uses budgets and MCP compaction (it makes the tool data from MCP servers smaller) to keep token spend under control. On a measured Claude Code task, it used 30 to 60 percent fewer tokens.

## What does a gated tool call look like?

Here is how a gateway can handle the calls of a fintech support agent. Good calls pass. Malicious or mistaken calls stop.

| Proposed call | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `look_up_order` for the customer in the session | Tool allowed, ID belongs to the user | Passes |
| `issue_refund` within the agent's limit | Schema and business rules pass | Passes |
| `issue_refund` above the limit | Needs human approval | Held for a reviewer |
| `send_reply` to an unknown outside address | Egress policy | Blocked |
| `run_shell` with a download command | Not on the allow-list | Blocked |
| The same search repeated in a loop | Budget cap | Throttled |

Every row, passed or blocked, leaves a signed receipt (a record of the call and the decision). Pavii hash-chains those receipts: each receipt holds a fingerprint of the receipt before it. Pavii anchors the chain on Hyper 0X, so an audit can show exactly what the agent tried and what the gateway decided. The figure above shows the same idea across all six gates. [Proof of execution for AI](../proof-of-execution-ai/) explains why the receipts matter.

## Where should you start?

1. List every tool that each agent can call today. Include the tools that MCP servers expose. Our post on [MCP server security risks](../mcp-server-security-risks/) shows what to look for.
2. Cut each agent down to an allow-list for its task.
3. Add strict schemas and business-rule checks to every tool that writes, sends or pays.
4. Move credentials into a gateway. Then set egress rules and budgets.
5. Require human approval for irreversible actions. Keep tamper-evident receipts (records that show any change).

For the full threat picture, see our guide [How to Secure AI Agents](../how-to-secure-ai-agents/). Pavii applies all six gates to every tool call. Our [AI-agent security](../../services/ai-agent-security/) team can help you roll it out. Book a call to see it on your own agents.

## What Is an AI Bill of Materials (AI-BOM)?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/ai-bill-of-materials/

An AI bill of materials (AI-BOM) is an inventory of every part that your AI agents depend on. It lists each model, adapter, dataset, code package, MCP server and skill, with its version, source and licence. It also records a hash (a digital fingerprint) of each part, so you can see any change. A dependency gate then uses the AI-BOM to block a part that is unknown, renamed or altered.

## What is in an AI supply chain?

An AI supply chain is every part that you did not build but your agents still run. Most teams think of code packages first. An AI agent (an AI model that uses tools to act) depends on much more:

- **Models:** the base model and any tuned versions of it.
- **Adapters:** small add-on files that change how a model behaves.
- **Datasets:** the data that trains, tunes or tests a model.
- **Packages:** code libraries that the agent or its tools install.
- **MCP servers:** services that give an agent its tools. Our post on [MCP server security risks](../mcp-server-security-risks/) covers them in detail.
- **Skills:** packaged instructions and scripts that an agent loads for one kind of task.
- **Prompt templates:** the files that format instructions for the model.

Agents often fetch these parts while they run, with no review. One fake or altered part can give an attacker code execution inside your systems. It can also hide a backdoor in your model.

## How do attackers get into an AI supply chain?

Attackers aim at the moments when a system trusts a name instead of the part itself. Six routes stand out.

1. **Look-alike names.** An attacker publishes `reqeusts` next to the popular `requests` package. Then the attacker waits for a typo.
2. **Package names that models invent.** A model suggests a package that does not exist. An attacker registers that name first, so the next install runs the attacker's code. Some people call this slopsquatting. Our post on [why AI agents act on hallucinations](../ai-agent-hallucination-risk/) covers the wider problem.
3. **Reused model names.** An author deletes an account on a model hub. An attacker registers the same name and uploads a different model. Every pipeline that loads the model by name now gets the attacker's file.
4. **Tampered adapters and chat templates.** A changed adapter or chat template can add a hidden trigger. The model behaves normally until a certain phrase appears.
5. **Malicious skills.** A skill can hide instructions for the model, or run scripts with the rights of the agent. This is a form of [prompt injection](../what-is-prompt-injection/) that arrives as an installed part.
6. **A compromised build pipeline.** An attacker who gets into the build system of a real project can ship a poisoned release. That release carries the real name and a valid signature.

## What goes into an AI-BOM?

An AI-BOM answers one question for every part: what is it, exactly, and where did it come from? For each part, record these facts:

- the name and the exact version
- the hash of the file
- the source: the registry, the model hub or the repository
- the publisher, and the signature if there is one
- the licence and the terms of use
- the owner inside your company, and the agents that use the part

Many teams already keep a software bill of materials (SBOM) for their code. An AI-BOM adds the parts that only AI systems have: models, adapters, datasets, MCP servers, skills and prompt templates. Keep it in a machine-readable format. Then a gate can read it at install time.

## Why pin by hash, not by name or "latest"?

A hash is a short digital fingerprint of a file. If one byte of the file changes, the hash changes too. A name or a "latest" tag points to whatever the publisher uploads next. A hash points to one exact file.

So pin each part to its hash. A silent update, a reused model name or a tampered adapter then cannot slip in. The new file has a different hash, and the gate refuses it until someone approves the change.

Apply the same rule to tools. The model reads each tool description as guidance, so a changed description can change the behaviour of the agent. Keep a hash of every tool definition, and approve the tool again when that hash changes.

## What does a signature prove, and what does it not prove?

A signature proves who published a part. It also proves that nobody changed the part after the publisher signed it. It stops a stranger from passing off a file as the work of a known publisher, and it catches tampering on the way to you.

A signature does not prove that a part is safe. A compromised build pipeline signs a poisoned release with the real key. A malicious publisher signs malware with their own key. So treat a valid signature as one check among several. Pair it with a pinned hash and a sandbox install. For models, add behaviour tests before you promote a new version.

## How does a dependency gate decide?

A dependency gate is a checkpoint that every new part must pass before an agent can use it. It reads the AI-BOM and gives one of three answers: allow, block or hold for a person. The figure shows five example requests as they move through the gate.

Each layer has one job:

1. **An agent asks for a part.** The request can be a package, a model, an adapter, an MCP server or a skill.
2. **Allow-list.** The gate checks the part against the approved list. A new part, such as the new `jira-helper` MCP server, waits for a person to review it.
3. **Look-alike names.** The gate blocks a name that copies a popular part. `reqeusts` looks like `requests`, so it stops here.
4. **Hash and signature.** The part must match its pinned hash and carry a valid signature. Version 2 of a model adapter has a different hash from the pinned one, so it stops here.
5. **Sandbox install.** Install scripts and network calls run in isolation first. The install script of `fast-csv-pro` calls an outside server, so the gate stops it.

Only `requests` at its pinned version passes every layer. The part, its hash and the decision then join the AI bill of materials on Hyper 0X. Every team reads the same inventory, and you can only add to it.

## Why anchor the AI-BOM on a blockchain?

A spreadsheet or an internal database can hold an AI-BOM. The problem is trust. Anyone with admin rights can edit it, and a partner cannot check it. A blockchain (a shared ledger that you can only add to) such as [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/) changes the picture in four ways:

- **Shared.** Every team and partner checks the same pinned hashes.
- **Append-only.** Each change to the allow-list is a new transaction with an approver. Nobody can quietly rewrite the list.
- **Time-stamped.** You can show which version of a part your team approved on a given date.
- **Open to partners.** Partner companies can share one vetted list and check it without access to your systems.

Be clear about the limit. The chain shows the origin of a part, and it shows that nobody altered the part after approval. It cannot tell you whether the part is safe. A poisoned release that you approve by mistake stays on the record as approved. Even then, the AI-BOM lists the agents that use the part, so you know where to look first.

## How does Pavii fit into the AI supply chain?

[Pavii](../../products/pavii/) is our security gateway for AI agents. Every agent call passes through it. Its supply chain gate puts the dependency-gate idea into practice. Every new package or MCP server must pass an allow-list, a pinned hash or a sandbox test.

Like every Pavii decision, the result gets a receipt. A receipt is a signed record of one decision, chained to the receipt before it. Pavii anchors that chain on Hyper 0X, so a deleted entry shows as a gap. [Proof of execution for AI](../proof-of-execution-ai/) explains how a receipt chain works.

Pavii does not scan model weights for backdoors, and it does not test model behaviour. Pair Pavii with your own model evaluation process for that work.

## Where should you start?

1. List every model, adapter, dataset, package, MCP server and skill that your agents use.
2. Record the version, hash, source and licence of each part.
3. Pin each part to its hash. Remove "latest" tags.
4. Route every install through one dependency gate with an allow-list and a sandbox.
5. Anchor the AI-BOM, and each change to it, on a shared record that you can only add to.

For the other risks that agents bring, read [How to Secure AI Agents](../how-to-secure-ai-agents/). A bad tool can also drain your budget, as our post on [denial of wallet](../denial-of-wallet-ai/) shows. Book a call with a Buckleson engineer to build your first AI-BOM.

## Asset Tokenization: How to Launch Tokenized Real-World Assets

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/asset-tokenization-guide/

Asset tokenization turns the ownership of a real-world asset into a digital token on a blockchain (a shared digital ledger). The asset, such as gold, a fund, an invoice or a property, stays with a custodian. Each token represents a share of that asset. Investors can then buy, hold and trade the tokens instantly and in small amounts. Every transfer settles on one verifiable record.

## Why do companies tokenize assets?

- **Smaller tickets.** You can split a gold bar or a building into thousands of affordable pieces.
- **Faster settlement.** Trades settle in one step, not after days of back-office reconciliation.
- **New investors.** You can sell tokens through apps and wallets that people already use.
- **Built-in compliance.** Rules such as KYC (know your customer) checks, investor limits and lock-ups run automatically.
- **Transparency.** The record shows every holder and every transfer. The custodian gives proof of reserve, that is, evidence that the real asset covers the tokens.

## What are the five steps to launch a tokenized asset?

The diagram above shows the full flow on Hyper 0X, the Buckleson blockchain. Do these steps in this order:

### 1. Structure and custody

Choose the legal wrapper. This is often a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) or a fund. Then choose a custodian to hold the real asset. Audits and proof of reserve start at this step.

### 2. Issue the token

Mint (create) tokens one-to-one with the asset in custody. On Hyper 0X, you mint them on your own private L2 (a private blockchain that settles on a main chain). Because the L2 is yours, you set the rules and keep investor data private.

### 3. Write the compliance rules

Write KYC status, country restrictions, investor limits and maker-checker approvals as code. In a maker-checker approval, one person makes a change and a second person approves it. Hyper 0X checks these rules **before** a transfer executes. As a result, a non-compliant trade never happens in the first place.

### 4. Distribute

Investors buy through [Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/) or through your own branded app. You build that app with our wallet SDKs (software development kits). Users can sign in without seed phrases (lists of backup words for a wallet) because of [account abstraction](../account-abstraction-no-seed-phrases/).

### 5. Trade and settle

A secondary market lets holders trade. Trades settle atomically: both legs (the payment and the asset transfer) complete, or neither does. As a result, no one is left holding cash without the asset. Read more in [atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/).

## Do tokens stay locked to one chain?

No. Bridges connect your L2 to public chains such as Ethereum and other EVM networks, Solana and Sui. A bridge moves tokens between two chains. Each bridge uses k-of-n signers: k of its n signers must approve a transfer. Your tokens can then reach wider liquidity when your rules allow it.

## What should you watch out for?

- **Custody first.** A token is only as good as the asset and the custodian behind it.
- **Rules before trades.** If you check compliance after a trade, you must unwind the bad trades.
- **Privacy.** Encrypt investor records per party. Do not make them visible to every node (every computer that runs the network).
- **Long-term security.** Ownership records can last for decades. Use [post-quantum-resistant](../post-quantum-resistant-blockchain/) cryptography.

## How does Buckleson help?

We design the token, the private L2, the compliance rules, the wallet and the market as one system on Hyper 0X. [H0X Pay](../../products/h0x-pay/) is coming soon. It will let everyday users invest a slice of every payment in tokenized gold, funds and stocks. To launch your own tokenized asset, see our [blockchain development services](../../services/asset-tokenization/) or book a call.

## Blockchain Data Encryption: The Four Layers That Matter

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/blockchain-data-encryption-four-layers/

Blockchains do not encrypt data by default. Public chains use hashes (short fingerprints of data) and digital signatures to prove that data is genuine, but anyone can read the transactions. To keep business data private, encryption must cover four places. These are: in transit between machines, in use during processing, on the ledger (the shared record) itself, and at rest on disk. Hyper 0X applies all four, so a failure at one layer does not expose the data.

## Why is blockchain data not private by default?

Public blockchains are open by design: anyone can check every transaction. Hashes prove that nobody has changed a record, and signatures prove who sent it. Neither hides what the record says. Addresses look anonymous, but chain analysis can often link them to real people and companies.

There is a second problem: replication. Every validator (a computer that checks and records transactions) keeps a full copy of the ledger, often for years. Each copy is another place that data can leak from. Think of a bank that records client positions, an asset issuer that holds investor details, or an AI team that logs prompts. For them, plain-text records on a shared ledger are not acceptable. That is why teams must design encryption in, layer by layer.

## What does encryption in transit protect against?

Data in transit is data that moves between machines: from a wallet to an app, from an app to a validator, or between validators. There are three threats: eavesdropping, tampering with messages on the way, and **harvest now, decrypt later**. In harvest now, decrypt later, an attacker records encrypted traffic today. Then the attacker waits for a quantum computer that can break it.

On [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), every connection uses TLS 1.3, the standard protocol for encrypted connections, with a hybrid key exchange. Key exchange is how two machines agree on a secret key over an open network. Hyper 0X combines classic X25519 with ML-KEM-768, the post-quantum algorithm that NIST published as FIPS 203 in August 2024. So an attacker must break both. AES-256-GCM encrypts the traffic itself. We explain the quantum side in more detail in [what makes a blockchain post-quantum-resistant](../post-quantum-resistant-blockchain/).

## What is encryption in use?

To process data, computers normally decrypt it in memory. At that moment, the data is most exposed. A compromised server, an insider with access to the machine, or another workload on the same hardware can read it. Encryption in use aims to let systems work on data but keep the plaintext (the readable data) from anyone without access rights.

The industry uses several techniques for this. They include trusted execution environments (hardware-isolated areas of a processor) and multi-party computation (parties compute a result together without sharing their inputs). Another technique is homomorphic encryption (computation on data that stays encrypted). Each has its own trade-offs in speed and complexity.

On Hyper 0X, computation runs with per-party keys. The data of each party opens only with the key of that party. So when Hyper 0X processes the transaction of one client, other parties on the network do not see its plaintext.

## How is data encrypted on the ledger?

The ledger is the shared, permanent record, so it needs protection that lasts as long as the data does. Hyper 0X writes two things for each record:

1. A **hash commitment**: a fingerprint that proves exactly what the ledger recorded and when, but does not reveal it.
2. A **per-party encrypted payload**: the contents, encrypted separately for each party to the record, with keys that only those parties hold.

Validators can order and record the transaction and its commitment, but they cannot read the contents. Later, either party can prove to an auditor what the parties agreed. To do this, the party reveals the data and shows that it matches the commitment. This layer protects against other participants, curious validators and anyone who gets a copy of the ledger. It is a big part of why a [permissioned blockchain](../permissioned-vs-permissionless-blockchain/), where only approved organisations run validators, can carry regulated data at all.

## What does encryption at rest add?

Data at rest is data stored on disks, in databases, in backups and in snapshots. The threats are physical and operational: a stolen drive, a leaked backup or a misconfigured storage bucket.

Hyper 0X uses AES-256-GCM **envelope encryption**. It encrypts each piece of data with its own data key. Master keys in hardware security modules (HSMs) then encrypt those data keys. An HSM is a tamper-resistant device that does encryption and never lets its keys out. GCM is a type of authenticated encryption: it also detects if someone has changed stored data. Envelope encryption also makes key rotation (a regular change of master keys) practical: you re-wrap the data keys and do not re-encrypt all the data.

## How do the four layers work together?

Each layer assumes that the layer before it has already failed. If an attacker gets past the network, the ledger is still encrypted. If someone steals a disk, the data on it is still ciphertext.

| Layer | Where the data is | Main threat | How Hyper 0X protects it |
|---|---|---|---|
| In transit | Moving between machines | Eavesdropping, tampering, harvest now, decrypt later | TLS 1.3, hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768, AES-256-GCM |
| In use | In processing | Compromised node, insider, neighbouring workload | Per-party keys during computation |
| On the ledger | In the shared record | Other participants and validators who read it | Hash commitments and per-party encrypted payloads |
| At rest | On disks and in backups | Stolen drives, leaked backups | AES-256-GCM envelope encryption, HSM-held master keys |

Think of an asset issuer that runs a tokenized bond on its own private L2. A private L2 is a private blockchain for one application. An investor places an order, and the order travels over hybrid post-quantum-resistant TLS. Hyper 0X processes the trade under per-party keys. The ledger records a commitment and a payload that only the investor and the issuer can read. The disks of the validators store all of it under AES-256-GCM, with master keys in HSMs.

An attacker who taps the network, reads a copy of the ledger or steals a backup sees only ciphertext and fingerprints. Read the [asset tokenization guide](../asset-tokenization-guide/) for the rest of that flow.

## Where should you start?

1. Map your data. Note what goes on-chain, who the parties are and how long each record must stay confidential.
2. Keep personal data off-chain where you can. Store commitments and references on the ledger instead.
3. Decide who holds the keys at each layer. Parties must hold their own payload keys. Master keys belong in HSMs.
4. Put records with a long legal life first in line for post-quantum-resistant key exchange.
5. Test each layer on its own. Assume that the layer has failed. Then check what an attacker can see.

Hyper 0X applies all four layers by default on every private L2. Our [custom blockchain team](../../services/custom-blockchains/) can map them to your data. Book a call to walk through your records layer by layer.

## Blockchain Finality Explained: When Is a Payment Final?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/blockchain-finality-explained/

Finality is the point after which nobody can change or reverse a blockchain transaction. On chains with probabilistic finality, such as Bitcoin, a payment only gets harder to undo as the chain adds more blocks on top. On chains with deterministic finality, a payment is final at the moment the chain confirms it. For payments and settlement, that difference decides when you can safely release goods, funds or securities.

## What does finality mean on a blockchain?

In banking, settlement finality is the moment a transfer becomes irrevocable and unconditional. It is a legal idea as much as a technical one. The CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures are the global standard for payment and settlement systems. They give finality a principle of its own (Principle 8). Principle 8 asks for final settlement that is clear and certain, at the latest by the end of the value date. The value date is the day the payment is due.

On a blockchain, finality is the guarantee that consensus will never remove a transaction from the record. Consensus is the process by which the computers of a network agree on the record. Different chains give that guarantee in very different ways. Some only make a probabilistic promise.

## What is probabilistic finality?

On proof-of-work chains like Bitcoin, miners compete to add the next block. Sometimes two miners find a block at almost the same moment. Then the network briefly has two competing versions of history. Nodes (the computers that run the network) follow the chain with the most accumulated work. The network drops the losing block, and with it any transactions that existed only in that block.

Each new block on top of the block with your payment makes a replacement far less likely. But the chance never reaches zero. That is why exchanges and merchants choose how many confirmations to wait for. Each block that includes or follows the payment is one confirmation. For large amounts on Bitcoin, a common rule of thumb is six confirmations, about an hour. The business must choose its own level of risk.

## What is a reorg, and why is it dangerous?

A reorg, short for chain reorganisation, happens when the network replaces recent blocks with a competing version. One-block reorgs happen naturally and are usually harmless. Deep reorgs are different. An attacker who controls most of the mining power of a network can secretly build a longer chain. Then the attacker releases it. People call this a 51 percent attack.

That makes a double spend possible: the attacker spends the same money twice. The attacker pays a merchant and waits for the goods. Then the attacker publishes a version of history where the payment never happened. Ethereum Classic, a smaller proof-of-work chain, suffered several such attacks in 2020. For a business, the result is a payment that showed as confirmed and then disappeared. The goods are already gone, and the books no longer match.

## What is deterministic finality?

Deterministic finality comes from Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) consensus. In BFT, a known set of validators (the computers that check and approve transactions) vote. They do not race to add blocks. When more than two thirds agree, the transaction is final. There are no competing chains to choose between, so there is nothing to reorganise. BFT protocols stay safe while fewer than one third of validators are faulty or dishonest.

The honest trade-off is this: if more than a third of validators go offline, a BFT network pauses. It does not split into two histories. It chooses to be correct rather than to keep moving. For financial records, a brief pause is far better than a wrong ledger. BFT works with a defined set of validators, so it fits naturally with [permissioned blockchains](../permissioned-vs-permissionless-blockchain/), where every validator is a known organisation.

Ethereum sits in between. Since its move to proof of stake, in which validators lock up ETH as a deposit, it has **economic finality**. Ethereum finalises blocks at checkpoints, about 13 minutes later. To reverse a finalised block, attackers must give up a large share of all staked ETH.

| Topic | Probabilistic | Economic | Deterministic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example | Bitcoin | Ethereum (proof of stake) | Hyper 0X, CometBFT chains |
| When is it final? | Never absolutely, but safer with each block | At checkpoints, about 13 minutes later | As soon as it is confirmed |
| Can reorgs happen? | Yes | Yes, before finalisation | No |
| What the business must do | Pick a confirmation count and accept some risk | Wait for finalisation | Act on confirmation |

## What does final in one pass mean?

[Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/) uses **aBFT**, asynchronous Byzantine fault tolerance. "Byzantine" means that validators can lie or misbehave, not only crash. "Asynchronous" means that the protocol makes no assumption about how quickly messages arrive. So it still reaches agreement when the network is slow or under attack.

Its consensus is hashgraph-based and leaderless. Leaderless means that there is no single block proposer that an attacker can bribe, censor or knock offline. It stays safe while fewer than one third of validators are faulty. Transaction order comes from the median time at which validators received each transaction. So no single node can front-run (put its own transaction ahead of others).

When the validators reach agreement, the transaction is final. There is no second stage in which you wait for more blocks to bury it. That is what we mean by final in one pass.

The same is true across layers. On Hyper 0X, each application runs on a private L2: a private blockchain that settles on the main chain, the L1. Each L2 posts its state roots (short fingerprints of its records) to the L1. The L1 never rolls back, so the shared record never rolls back either. For more about how the layers fit together, read [layer 1 vs layer 2 blockchain](../layer-1-vs-layer-2-blockchain/).

## Why does finality matter for payments and settlement?

Every payment flow has a moment when someone releases value because they believe that the payment has arrived. Finality decides if that belief is safe.

- **When to release value.** A merchant ships goods, a broker delivers securities, and a lender releases funds. Each one must act only after the incoming payment is final.
- **Both legs of a trade.** An exchange of an asset for payment in one step protects you only if nobody can undo that step. That is the basis of [atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/).
- **Reconciliation.** With probabilistic finality, a payment can show as confirmed and then as unconfirmed. Then operations teams must chase it. With deterministic finality, [Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/) users see only three states: pending, confirmed or failed.
- **Liquidity.** Uncertain finality makes firms wait longer or hold extra buffers. Certainty lets them use funds again as soon as a payment settles.

Think of a fintech that pays merchants in several countries. On a chain with probabilistic finality, its treasury team must choose a confirmation count and accept the remaining risk. The other choice is to wait longer and tie up cash. If a reorg happens after a payout, the team must try to get the money back. With deterministic finality, each payout is either confirmed and final, or it failed. The ledger matches the bank statement.

## Where should you start?

1. Map every point in your flows where you release value after you receive a payment.
2. For each chain that you use, find out which finality model it has. Read what "confirmed" means in its documentation.
3. Ask what happens if a third of the validators go offline. Does the network pause, or can it fork (split into two histories)?
4. Check your bridges (the links that move assets between chains). A cross-chain transfer is only as final as the least final chain it passes through.
5. Write your finality rule into policy. Then operations teams know exactly when to act.

On Hyper 0X, every confirmed transaction is final in one pass, from the L1 to every private L2. Book a call to see how that fits your payment or settlement flows.

## Blockchain Payments for Merchants: How to Accept Them

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/blockchain-payments-for-merchants/

To accept blockchain payments, a merchant shows the customer a payment request, and the customer pays from their own wallet. The request is usually a QR code, a link or an invoice with the amount and a wallet address. After the network makes the payment final, the money sits in the merchant's wallet. A chargeback (a forced refund through the card network) cannot pull it back. Many merchants choose stablecoins (tokens with a steady value) to avoid price swings, then keep them or convert them to local currency. The key decisions are which assets and networks to accept, how to treat finality and refunds, and whether to use a gateway or build in-house.

## How does a blockchain payment work at checkout?

The flow looks different from a card payment, but it is simple:

1. **Create a payment request.** Your system generates an invoice. The invoice shows the amount, the asset (for example a dollar stablecoin), the network, a wallet address, a reference and an expiry time.
2. **Show it to the customer.** Online, that is a button or link. In a shop, it is a QR code on a screen or receipt.
3. **The customer pays.** They scan or click, check the amount in their wallet and approve. Their wallet broadcasts the transaction.
4. **Watch the network.** Your gateway or your own node (a server that follows the network) sees the transaction arrive. It matches the transaction to the invoice by address or reference.
5. **Wait for finality.** When no one can reverse the payment, mark the order as paid. Then release the goods.
6. **Settle your way.** Keep the funds in a business wallet, pay suppliers with them, or convert them to your local currency.

## What is the difference between settlement and finality?

Settlement is when money actually moves to you. Finality is the point after which no one can undo a payment. With cards, the two are far apart. A card payment gets approval in seconds. But funds usually reach the merchant one to three business days later. The customer can also file a chargeback months after that.

On a blockchain, settlement and finality arrive together. The speed depends on the network:

- **Probabilistic finality.** On Bitcoin, each new block makes a payment harder to reverse. A common rule for large amounts is to wait for six confirmations, about an hour.
- **Checkpoint finality.** Ethereum finalizes blocks after two epochs (fixed groups of blocks), roughly 13 minutes.
- **Deterministic finality.** Some chains use Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) consensus, a voting method that still works when some validators fail or cheat. These chains treat a transaction as final when the network confirms it. [Hyper 0X](../../products/hyper-0x/), the Buckleson blockchain, works this way: final in one pass, with no reorganizations (rewrites of recent blocks).

For a coffee, a merchant can accept a payment the moment it appears. For a car, wait for finality. Set a policy per order size. Our post [blockchain finality explained](../blockchain-finality-explained/) goes deeper.

## How do blockchain payments compare with card payments?

| Topic | Card payment | Blockchain payment |
|---|---|---|
| When funds settle | Usually one to three business days | At network finality, from seconds to about an hour |
| Chargebacks | Yes, often months later | No, the merchant sends any refunds |
| Typical costs | Interchange, scheme and processor fees | Network fee plus any gateway and conversion fees |
| Cross-border | Currency conversion and extra fees | The same flow worldwide, with conversion only at the edges |
| What the customer needs | A card | A wallet holding the asset |

## Why do many merchants prefer stablecoins?

A stablecoin is a token designed to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar or one euro. Reserves such as cash and short-term government debt back the most widely used ones. USDC and USDT are the largest dollar stablecoins. If you accept them, a $100 order is still worth about $100 when you settle. That is not true of Bitcoin or Ether.

Regulation is also catching up. In the EU, the stablecoin rules of the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) started to apply in June 2024. In the United States, the GENIUS Act of 2025 set federal rules for payment stablecoins. Still, check who issues each stablecoin and how the issuer holds and reports its reserves. Also check which networks it runs on.

## What fees should merchants expect?

Blockchain payments remove card interchange (the fee that the card-issuing bank takes), but they are not free. Budget for:

- **Network fees.** Each transaction pays a fee to the network, often called gas. The amount depends on the chain and how busy it is. Some apps pay this fee for their users.
- **Gateway fees.** Payment processors usually charge per transaction or per month.
- **Conversion costs.** When you convert stablecoins into local currency, you pay a spread (the gap between buy and sell prices) or a fee. Bank transfer costs come on top.
- **Operations.** Wallet security, reconciliation and accounting take staff time.

Compare the total cost per order. Remember that blockchain payments also remove chargeback fees and the fraud losses linked to them.

## How do refunds and disputes work without chargebacks?

Customers cannot reverse a payment, so refunds become the merchant's job. Send the refund in the same asset to an address that the customer confirms. Record the link to the original order. If you refund in a volatile coin, decide in advance how you handle price changes. Your published refund policy and local consumer protection law still apply.

## What about compliance, tax and accounting?

If you use a gateway that holds funds for you, it usually does three things:

- It runs KYC (know-your-customer) checks on your business.
- It screens payments against sanctions lists.
- It follows the FATF Travel Rule. This rule requires crypto service providers to share sender and recipient details for transfers between them.

For accounting, record the value of each payment in local currency at the time you received it. Tax treatment varies by country, so involve your accountant before launch.

## Should you use a payment gateway or build your own?

Imagine an online electronics retailer that sells to customers in 30 countries. A hosted gateway gets it live quickly, but the gateway can hold the funds and set the rules. An in-house build gives full control, but the retailer must then run wallets, nodes and reconciliation. A middle path is a wallet SDK (software development kit). This is a set of ready-made wallet and payment components that the retailer embeds under its own brand. See [what a wallet SDK is](../what-is-a-wallet-sdk/) and [how to launch your own crypto wallet](../how-to-launch-a-crypto-wallet/).

Settlement design matters too. Say the retailer converts stablecoins to another asset, or pays a supplier in a swap. Both sides must move together. [Atomic settlement](../atomic-settlement/) means that both legs complete in one step, or neither does. Then no one is left exposed.

## Where does H0X Pay fit?

[H0X Pay](../../products/h0x-pay/) is coming soon from Buckleson. It will let you pay and get paid in crypto with links, QR codes and invoices, settled on Hyper 0X. It will also let you invest a small slice of every payment in tokenized assets, starting with gold. Payments are a later phase of the H0X Pay roadmap. The [Hyper Wallet SDKs](../../products/hyper-wallet/) are also under development. They are designed to give businesses a branded checkout with payments and a payment gateway.

## Where should you start?

1. Pick one stablecoin and one or two networks that your customers already use.
2. Write a finality policy: how long to wait before you release goods, by order size.
3. Choose a gateway, a wallet SDK or an in-house build. Decide who holds the keys.
4. Agree refund rules, accounting treatment and tax handling with your finance team.
5. Run a pilot with a small share of orders before the full rollout.

For branded payments, see our [wallet SDK services](../../services/wallet-sdks/). H0X Pay is under development and coming soon. Book a call to learn more.

## Custodial vs Non-Custodial Wallets: Which to Offer?

URL: https://buckleson.com/blog/custodial-vs-non-custodial-wallet/

In a custodial wallet, a company holds the private keys and moves funds for the user, much as a bank holds deposits. A non-custodial wallet keeps the keys on the user's own device, so only the user can move the assets. A custodial wallet is easier to recover, but it brings licensing duties and counterparty risk (the risk that the provider fails). A non-custodial wallet removes that risk, but it puts recovery in the user's hands. That is why many fintechs offer non-custodial by default and add custody only where clients need it.

## What is the difference between a custodial and a non-custodial wallet?

A private key, a secret number that signs transactions, controls every crypto asset. Whoever holds the key controls the funds.

In a custodial wallet, the provider holds the keys, often in pooled wallets. Cold storage (keys kept offline) or hardware security modules (HSMs, tamper-resistant devices built to store keys) protect those wallets. The user sees an account balance, as on an exchange. In a non-custodial wallet, also called self-custody, the wallet creates and stores the key on the user's phone or hardware device. The provider supplies the software but cannot move the funds.

| Topic | Custodial | Non-custodial |
|---|---|---|
| Who holds the keys | The provider | The user, on their device |
| Who can move funds | The provider, on instruction | Only the user |
| If the provider fails | Funds can be frozen or lost | Funds stay with the user |
| Recovery | Identity check and support desk | Built into the wallet design |
| Licensing | Usually a regulated activity | Wallet software is often out of scope |
| Best for | Institutions and managed accounts | Retail users, apps, global reach |

## Who carries the risk in each model?

With custody, the user trusts the provider. If the provider suffers a hack, mismanages funds or goes bankrupt, customers can lose access. When the FTX exchange collapsed in November 2022, customers with balances on the platform were not able to withdraw them.

With self-custody, that counterparty risk disappears, but a different risk appears: the user can lose access. A lost phone or a missing backup can cost money. So can a phishing site, a fake site that tricks someone into signing a bad transaction. Nobody can reverse these losses. Good wallet design mostly shrinks this second risk without bringing back the first.

## What licenses does a custodial wallet need?

In most major markets, holding crypto for customers is a regulated activity, because it looks a lot like holding deposits. The details vary by country, so treat this as a map, not legal advice.

- **European Union.** MiCA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, makes custody and administration of crypto-assets for clients a licensed service. Providers must get authorization as crypto-asset service providers (CASPs). They must keep client assets segregated and maintain a custody policy. MiCA states that providers of non-custodial wallet hardware or software fall outside its scope.
- **United States.** The state and the business model decide whether a custodian needs money transmitter licenses, a New York BitLicense or a trust charter. Banks also follow guidance from their own regulators.
- **Anti-money-laundering rules.** The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) expects virtual asset service providers to verify customers. FATF also expects them to send sender and recipient details with transfers. This duty is the Travel Rule. FATF guidance says that businesses that only supply wallet software, and never control customer funds, are generally not virtual asset service providers.

A non-custodial wallet does not make an app regulation-free. Fiat on-ramps (services that change money into crypto), trading, lending or yield features can each bring their own requirements. But a core product without custody often avoids the heaviest duties: safeguarding client assets, capital requirements and the liability that comes with them.

## How does recovery work in each model?

Custodial recovery is familiar. The user proves who they are, often with the same identity checks used at sign-up, and the provider restores access.

Non-custodial recovery has changed a lot. The original method was a seed phrase: 12 to 24 words, defined by the BIP-39 standard, that can rebuild every key. It works, but people lose the words, photograph them or type them into fake sites. Newer approaches remove that burden:

1. **Passkeys and secure hardware.** Passkeys are sign-in keys that replace passwords. The phone's secure chip protects the keys. A face scan or fingerprint gives access to them.
2. **Smart accounts.** With account abstraction, the account is a smart contract (a program on the blockchain) that sets its own rules. The rules include who can help recover the account, such as a second device or trusted guardians. ERC-4337 brought this model to Ethereum and EVM chains (chains that run Ethereum-style smart contracts).
3. **Key splitting.** Multi-party computation (MPC) splits a key into shares, and different devices or parties hold the shares. No single loss is then fatal. One caution: if the provider holds enough shares to move funds alone, the wallet is custodial in practice, whatever the marketing says.

On Hyper 0X, account abstraction is the default: users sign in with a face scan or passkey and never handle a seed phrase. Read more in [account abstraction without seed phrases](../account-abstraction-no-seed-phrases/).

## Which model gives users a better experience?

For years, custodial won on convenience: email sign-in, password resets and no network fees to think about. Non-custodial meant seed phrases, gas tokens (the coins that pay network fees) and confusing errors. Account abstraction closes most of that gap. Apps can pay network fees for users, set spending limits and support recovery, while the keys stay with the user.

Self-custody also does things that custody struggles with. Users can connect to dApps (blockchain apps) through WalletConnect and hold assets from many chains in one place. They can also move funds without waiting for a provider to approve a withdrawal. [Hyper Wallet](../../products/hyper-wallet/) is an example: a non-custodial wallet and exchange in one app.

## Why do many fintechs choose non-custodial by default?

For a fintech, the default matters more than the option. Non-custodial by default means:

- **Less to safeguard.** There is no central pool of customer keys for attackers to target.
- **A lighter licensing path in many markets,** because the core wallet is software, not a custody service.
- **Room to grow.** You can switch on regulated features market by market as licenses arrive.
- **User trust.** People who watched exchanges fail value owning their keys.

Custody still has a place. Institutions, fund managers and corporate treasuries often must hold assets with a regulated custodian. Some retail users simply prefer an account they can reset. So the strongest setups are hybrid: non-custodial for everyone, with custody added for the clients and markets that need it, inside one app.

Take a payments fintech with a large retail base and a few corporate clients. It launches a non-custodial wallet for retail users, so it never holds their crypto. For corporate clients that need a custodian, it adds custody with maker-checker approvals (one person proposes a transfer and another approves it). Both groups use the same app and the same records.

That is how the Hyper Wallet SDKs work. The wallet is non-custodial out of the box. Businesses that need custody add it through the SDKs. If the term is new, start with [what a wallet SDK is](../what-is-a-wallet-sdk/).

## Where should you start?

1. Map your users: retail, institutional or both, and in which markets.
2. Get legal advice per market on custody, anti-money-laundering rules and the Travel Rule before you choose.
3. Default to non-custodial unless a client or regulator requires custody.
4. Design recovery first, with passkeys and account abstraction instead of seed phrases.
5. Pick an SDK that supports both models, so custody later is an add-on, not a rebuild. See [how to launch your own crypto wallet](../how-to-launch-a-crypto-wallet/) for build vs white-label.

Hyper Wallet and its SDKs give you a non-custodial wallet with optional custody, backed by our [wallet SDK services](../../services/wallet-sdks/). Book a call to map the right model for your users.
